data.content:
Samuel Pepys
The author and main narrator of the diary; identified in the title as M.A., F.R.S., Clerk of the Acts, and Secretary to the Admiralty. The entry records activities on June 1 and 2, 1661.<SEP>The diarist and narrator of the passage; practises singing, dines with My Lady, works at the office, visits Moorefields and Deptford, meets friends at the Bell, sleeps in the Nursery, and attends church.<SEP>Diarist who records his daily activities in July 1661, including household purchases, music practice, household concerns, and reporting to the Duke of York about the ships.<SEP>The diary writer and first-person narrator of the passage, who visits the Theatre, hears news of Robert Pepys, travels to Brampton, and records the surrounding events.<SEP>English diarist and central figure of the passage; records his travels, meetings, social visits, theatre attendance, borrowed money, and family interactions in July–August 1661.<SEP>Diarist and author of the diary; the narrator whose observations and actions are described in the text.

Diary of Samuel Pepys
The diary written by Samuel Pepys, covering in this section the entries for June, July, and August 1661. The text is transcribed from a shorthand manuscript and includes notes and editorial additions.

David Widger
Producer credited at the beginning of the presented text of the diary.

Mynors Bright
Transcriber of the diary from the shorthand manuscript; described as a late fellow and president of Magdalene College Cambridge.

Lord Braybrooke
Author of notes included in the edition of the diary.

Henry B. Wheatley
Editor of the diary who added additions to the text.

Lady Batten
Person referred to as “my Lady” in the text; she left with Sir W. Batten to keep Whitsuntide.<SEP>Wife of Sir W. Batten; reported out of town and therefore absent from the Sunday dinner.<SEP>A woman who traveled in a two-coach party with The Diarist to see Bartholomew Fayre.<SEP>Woman referred to as my Lady Batten; she was the subject of gossip that she had been the mistress of a man who left her his estate.<SEP>A woman who spent the afternoon at the Theatre with Sir W. Pen.<SEP>Lady mentioned in the same passage as the King, Duke, Duchess, and Madame Palmer.

Mr. Gauden
Companion of Pepys who traveled by water with Pepys and Sir W. Pen to Woolwich and Deptford.

Captain Poole
Person with whom Pepys and his companions dined at the tavern in Woolwich.<SEP>A captain from Jamaica who accompanies the narrator at Woolwich, visits the tavern, travels on the wherry, and parts from him near The Tower.

Mr. Creed
A companion of the Narrator who accompanies him back to the house and to the Towre, where they speak for ammunition.<SEP>Person whose £10,000 imprest bill was signed for the forthcoming voyage.<SEP>Mr. Creed is a man who dined with the narrator and later went with the narrator to a tobacco shop.<SEP>Person ordered by My Lord to imprest money on The Narrator, with payment to be made by Alderman Backwell.<SEP>The writer of a letter dated 15th July who reports that My Lord has recovered from pain and fever and expects to go aboard.

Mr. Mills
Preacher whose sermon Pepys heard at church on Whitsunday.<SEP>Parson of the parish of the diarist; took part in the late talk and disputation at Sir W. Batten's house.<SEP>A preacher who delivers a sermon on the necessity of restitution, which the Narrator and his wife attend.

Greatorex
Visitor to Pepys who discussed mathematics and demonstrated how levers gain strength at the expense of time.

Woolwich
Place reached by water where Pepys toured ships and dined with Captain Poole at the tavern.<SEP>A place on the Thames where the narrator goes ashore with Captain Poole, Mr. Kennersley, and others.<SEP>A place associated with Mr. Falconer in the diary account.

Deptford
Place Pepys visited by water to inspect ships and from which Pepys and companions walked to Redriffe.<SEP>Place reached by barge from Whitehall where The Narrator boards the Dutch Yacht.<SEP>The place where Samuel Pepys and the two Sir Williams went to examine the delays in getting ships ready.<SEP>The place where Sir G. Carteret invited officers to dinner.

Redriffe
Place to which Pepys and companions walked from Deptford, stopping at the half-way house on the way.

Whitsuntide
Christian holiday period referred to as Whitsunday and Whitsuntide; Sir W. Batten and Lady Batten left to keep it, and cakes were made for it.

Pepysian Library
Library at Magdalene College Cambridge where the shorthand manuscript of the diary was kept.

Magdalene College Cambridge
College with which Mynors Bright was associated and where the Pepysian Library is located.

Admiralty
Government body to which Samuel Pepys was secretary.

Whitsunday
The holy day on June 2, 1661; Pepys attended church services and heard Mr. Mills's sermon, which was fit for the day.

Mr. Townsend
An officer connected with the Wardrobe whose possible death is discussed as a contingency in arranging the Wardrobe business.<SEP>Mr. Townsend is a man ordered by My Lord to reveal the whole mystery of the Wardrobe to the narrator.<SEP>Person at The Wardrobe willing to communicate anything for My Lord's advantage concerning My Lord's business.<SEP>Mr. Townsend is a friend who was present at the Wardrobe for Lord of Sandwich's birthday and who was called after dinner.<SEP>A man who dines in a merry company with his wife, receives a call from Captain Cooke, and goes with the Narrator and Captain Cooke to a tavern.

Mr. Young
The holder of a place in the Wardrobe for which the Narrator desires the refusal in case the place falls vacant.

Cousin Scott
A male relative of the Narrator who comes with Narrator's Father to dine at the house.

Father Bowyer
A person referred to as "my father Bowyer" who arrives during the Narrator's dinner with a party of relatives and friends.

Sir W. Batten
Sir W. Batten was a contemporary of Samuel Pepys and a frequent participant in the diarist’s social life. He hosted numerous gatherings at his house, including a Sunday dinner after church, at which Pepys and other guests were present; a post-theater evening where Pepys and companions stayed late; and a gathering with Pepys, the Comptroller, and Mr. Mills, who sat late talking and disputing. Batten also hosted a convivial occasion where Pepys and others ate a venison pasty and were merry. Pepys often visited and sat with Batten at his home, indicating an ongoing personal acquaintance.

Batten had several notable interactions with Pepys beyond dining. On one occasion, Batten left in the morning with Lady Batten to keep Whitsuntide, and Pepys took leave of him. That same night, Pepys borrowed £40 from Batten. Batten also waited alongside Pepys on the Duke of York, showing his involvement in court or official business. Pepys sought Batten at the Dolphin tavern and later found him there; on another occurrence, Batten was found at the Dolphin, where Pepys and Sir W. Pen joined him. Pepys also visited Batten at his house with wine. Additionally, Batten’s home was the destination when Pepys and others were called to see the great baboon that Captain Holmes had brought from Guiny. Thus, Sir W. Batten appears as a host, acquaintance, and occasional lender to Pepys within the diary’s social and professional circles.

Dr. Peirce
A doctor who goes over to the Beare at the Bridge Foot with the Narrator in the morning, expecting to meet Lord Hinchinbroke.<SEP>A companion who goes with the narrator to the Beare at the Bridge Foot and later to the Wardrobe.

Lord Hinchinbroke
A nobleman whom the Narrator and Dr. Peirce think they will meet at the Beare at the Bridge Foot.<SEP>A nobleman planning to set forth for France with a brother; the departure is postponed because Lord Abbot Montagu is not in Paris.

data.entity_name: The Beare at the Bridge Foot
data.content:
The Beare at the Bridge Foot
The house or tavern at the bridge foot where the Narrator and Dr. Peirce go in the morning.

The Towre
The fortified place called "the Towre," where the Narrator and Mr. Creed go to request ammunition and around which they walk.

Narrator
The Narrator is the unnamed first-person diarist of the diary passage and the central figure through whom all events, actions, and observations are recounted. The Narrator is male: he is the husband of Narrator’s Wife and the son of Narrator’s Father and Mother. He is entrusted by My Lord with overseeing affairs during My Lord’s absence and receives orders from the Lord Chancellor and Mr. Edward Montagu, working at the Office. He records daily activities including receiving instructions, hosting dinner guests, dining with My Lady, and managing money, goods, and household matters.

The Narrator’s travels and business are extensively documented. He journeys along the Thames to Greenwich, Woolwich, and Whitehall, and makes overland trips by horseback to Ware, Barkway, Brampton, Cambridge, and Impington. He visits his father, deals with an uncle’s corpse and will, and works on uncle’s estate affairs, consulting Roger Pepys at the Assizes about the will. He is troubled by estate matters, walks around Portholme, and attends to correspondence with his father.

Socially and professionally, the Narrator dines with Lord Crew and My Lady, waits on the Duke of York, visits relatives, sick acquaintances, and family, attends church, and gives fruit and wine to visitors. He reads The Spanish Gypsey, hires the Margate Hoy, records boating trips and social meals, goes to the Opera, and visits a baboon. He also argues with Pall, settles Maid Jane’s service, handles family finances, discusses a proposed wife for Tom, expresses worry about Tom, and notes dissatisfaction with the Court and Clergy while intending to subscribe to the Benevolence. Throughout, the Narrator remains unnamed, yet his first-person perspective gives the diary its continuity and personal detail.

Narrator's House
The Narrator's house, where he dined with his father, Cousin Scott, and others, where the Bowyer party stayed all afternoon, and where he later walked with his wife.<SEP>The narrator's residence where goods are brought and stored overnight and where painters work on the stairs.<SEP>The narrator's home, which was being cleaned and which the narrator found very clean on the 21st and 22nd.<SEP>The Narrator's home, shown to Lady Jem and Pall; their mother had previously come alone with the Narrator's Wife to inspect it.<SEP>The narrator's dwelling where he gave fruit and wine to Lord Hinchingbroke on Saturday.<SEP>The Narrator's home, used as a place where My Lady sends her sons.

Sir W. Pen
Sir W. Pen was a knight and colleague of Samuel Pepys, frequently appearing in Pepys’s diary as a companion in both professional and social settings. He traveled by water with Pepys and Mr. Gauden to Woolwich and Deptford, rode with Pepys to Moorefields and later accompanied him to Deptford, and also came home with Pepys and his wife, drank with them, and had a daughter who had recently returned from Ireland. He was a guest at Sir W. Batten’s Sunday dinner.

In his official capacity, Sir W. Pen waited with Pepys on the Duke of York, and the two jointly reported Navy finances to the Duke. He transported Pepys and Captain Ferrers in his coach, and he socialized with Pepys at the Dolphin and at the Theatre. On one occasion he was at the Theatre with Lady Batten and later at the Dolphin, where Pepys followed him.

Sir W. Pen’s house was also a regular gathering place for Pepys and others, where they sat and drank until late, with one visit made at night. Pepys visited him on the 23rd after putting on mourning, and another account likewise describes the diarist visiting him while in mourning. Finally, Sir W. Pen was the recipient of a counterfeit letter written by Pepys to mock him about a stolen tankard.

Brother of Lord Hinchinbroke
The unnamed brother of Lord Hinchinbroke who is to travel with Lord Hinchinbroke to France.

Lord Abbot Montagu
A nobleman who is not in Paris when Lord Hinchinbroke and a brother plan to leave for France.

The Comptroller
An official who asks the narrator to inspect houses near the office and proposes a housing arrangement involving Mr. Turner, Mr. Davis, and the narrator.<SEP>Official who accompanied the diarist to Sir W. Batten's house and sat there late talking.<SEP>An unnamed official with the title Comptroller who goes with the Narrator to view Sir Rd. Ford’s house.

Mr. Turner
A man involved in the proposed housing arrangement; the Comptroller thinks of taking a house for Mr. Turner or himself and proposes that the narrator use Mr. Turner's lodgings.<SEP>An acquaintance from the narrator's office who is in Cambridge with Mr. Turner's Wife to settle the couple's son there; Mr. Turner meets the narrator at the Rose Tavern.

Mr. Davis
A man whose lodgings are included in the Comptroller's proposed housing arrangement.

J. Holcroft
Cousin of the narrator; met at the narrator's father's house and given wine at the Bear Tavern.

The Wardrobe
The Wardrobe was a royal office and department in London, staffed by officers such as Mr. Townsend and Mr. Young, whose business followed the instructions of My Lord. It also functioned as the London residence of My Lord and My Lady—understood to be the household of Edward Montagu, Earl of Sandwich—and served as a frequent setting for meals, visits, and family events in the diary of Samuel Pepys.

As a building, The Wardrobe was where My Lady lived and where Pepys often dined with her, sometimes accompanied by Dean Fuller, Dr. Thomas Pepys, or others. He also dined there with Mr. Moore, Ned Pickering, and Sir Robert Slingsby; on one occasion he arrived too late, dining with the servants before going to My Lady. It was a place reached by water, where Pepys met his wife, found My Young Lord ill, took leave of Lord Hinchingbroke and his brother before their trip to France, and learned that Lady Sandwich and her child were well. The Wardrobe hosted the celebration of the Earl of Sandwich’s birthday, and there Pepys and his wife visited My Lady when she lay confined to bed. The narrator also spent the night at The Wardrobe after calling there with Sir Robert Slingsby. It was thus both an official workplace and the central domestic hub of the Sandwich household, where Pepys conducted social, family, and administrative business throughout his diary.

Lord Crew
A dinner host who converses with the narrator about young noblemen and gentlemen considering going to sea as honorable service.<SEP>Host with whom the narrator dines and who, with Lady Crew, treats the narrator warmly.<SEP>A lord with whom the narrator dined; staying at Sir H. Wright's house while his own new house is being made fit for him and is troubled.<SEP>A nobleman who dines with the Narrator and is staying at Sir H. Wright's while a new house is prepared.

Queen Elizabeth
The queen in whose time the anecdote about a young nobleman waiting on Lord Bedford is set.

Young Lord of Kent
A young nobleman in the anecdote who waits on Lord Bedford and later inherits the Earldom of Kent.

Lord Bedford
A nobleman waited on by the Young Lord of Kent; Lord Bedford yields his seat to the Young Lord after the earldom passes.

France
The country that Lord Hinchinbroke and his brother plan to travel to.<SEP>France is the destination country of Lord Hinchingbroke and the young gentlemen's planned journey.<SEP>Country from which money was received by the sale of Dunkirk; proceeds were believed to fund L20,000 paid to the Chancellor.<SEP>Destination country of the journey made by Lord Hinchingbroke and the brother.

Paris
The city where Lord Abbot Montagu is not present when the travelers' plan is discussed.

Beare at the Bridge Foot
A place near the bridge where the narrator and Dr. Peirce go, expecting to meet Lord Hinchinbroke and his brother.

Bear Tavern
The tavern where the narrator gives wine to J. Holcroft, the narrator's father, and Tom.

Mr. Moore
Mr. Moore is an acquaintance, advisor, and close companion of the diarist Samuel Pepys, appearing frequently in Pepys’s personal and professional activities. Lord Sandwich (referred to as “My Lord”) intended to join Mr. Moore with Pepys in managing Wardrobe business during his absence. Mr. Moore was a companion at the Wardrobe, where Pepys shared a bed with him in Mr. Moore’s chamber. He also accompanied Pepys on numerous excursions, including to Westminster Hall, the Theatre (leaving from Pepys’s mother’s house), Fenchurch Street, and into the City, where they parted. On other occasions, Mr. Moore and Pepys hired a coach together to Chelsea to examine and seal a document with the Lord Privy Seal, drank together at a tavern near the Savoy and at the Mitre, and met at My Lady’s house before dining at the Wardrobe, where Mr. Moore informed Pepys that the next day was a Seal day.

Professionally, Mr. Moore acted as an advisor. At Pepys’s request, he sent advice that the three witnesses of a will being legatees would not invalidate the will. Pepys found him at home on one occasion, where Mr. Moore dined with Pepys and read his uncle’s will, offering an opinion on it. After Pepys’s deputation was accepted, Mr. Moore read over all the bills at White Hall. At Whitehall, he also told Pepys that Lady Sandwich had given birth to a daughter. Additionally, Mr. Moore gave Pepys a copy of Hooker’s Ecclesiastical Polity, which had been given the previous Wednesday. Through these varied interactions, Mr. Moore emerges as a trusted and frequent associate of Pepys in both business and social matters.

Harry the 4th
A play that the narrator sees at The Theatre and considers a good play.

Bank-side
The riverside stretch that the narrator and the Comptroller walk over on the way to the Temple.

The Temple
A place reached after walking over Bank-side; the narrator goes from there to his father's house.<SEP>A location where Sir H. Finch is reader and hosts the royal dinner.

Southwark
A district the narrator reaches by going over the water and walking over the fields on his way home from the Theatre.

My Lord
My Lord is the name Samuel Pepys uses for his noble patron, evidently Edward Montagu, the man appointed ambassador to bring over Katherine of Braganza and later chosen Master of Trinity House. He was a nobleman connected to households at Whitehall, the Wardrobe, and My Lady’s household, and Pepys acted as his servant and deputy, at one point being sworn as his deputy at the Privy Seal. My Lord was preparing for a sea voyage, for which Pepys obtained the signing of his imprest bill of £1,000. He was often at Whitehall conducting business, and gave Pepys instructions regarding the Wardrobe, especially concerning Mr. Townsend. He required £300 worth of cloth to be given as presents in Barbary, and cloth purchased by Pepys’s father was intended for him.

Before departing, My Lord took leave of the King, was seen off by Sir Robert Slingsby, and sailed aboard the Dutch Yacht, firing a five-gun salute to Pepys. He later stayed at the Wardrobe to take leave of friends and ordered household items to be sent after him. His mission included going to Algiers to settle business and put the fleet in order, then returning to Lisbon with three ships. During his absence, Pepys oversaw preparations and wrote letters to him, at times having no news of his whereabouts when reaching London. On one occasion My Lord was recovering from a fever and wind in his right side but was reported ready to go aboard within a day or two.

Pepys handled numerous matters for My Lord: he put his papers in order, wrote to him about completed business with My Lady’s household, and had letters ready for him, though some were not ready when Captain Isham called. My Lord also advised Pepys about a land purchase, sent him messages, and received a letter written late at night. He was not universally praised, however: when he was expected at the Privy Seal but failed to appear all afternoon, he was criticized for delaying business and treating clerks harshly. Overall, My Lord is depicted as Pepys’s influential and often absent patron, involved in naval, diplomatic, and household affairs.

Earldom of Kent
The noble title that, according to the anecdote told by Lord Crew, falls to the young Lord of Kent while he is serving Lord Bedford in Queen Elizabeth's time.

The Diarist
The unnamed writer of the diary entry who records personal activities such as giving money to the wife, dining at the Lord's lodgings, doing business at the office, playing bowls, drinking and singing with Sir William Pen, traveling to Greenwich with Captain Lambert, and visiting Mr. Holland's house in Bridewell.<SEP>First-person narrator of the diary entry. The Diarist is the husband of My Wife, receives advice from My Lord about money, and records visits and conversations.<SEP>The unnamed narrator of the diary, who attends to business, dines with acquaintances, practices music, sees a play, and plans to buy land.<SEP>First-person speaker of the diary passage; a London man who conducts office business, visits Westminster Hall, takes singing lessons, attends operas and plays, and has family members.<SEP>The person who writes the diary, referred to as "I"; he makes visits, attends the theatre, and deals with family and household matters.<SEP>The first-person narrator of the diary entry who waits on the Duke of York, dines with My Lady, attends the Theatre and the Opera, and receives letters from Mr. Creed.<SEP>The first-person narrator who accompanies the ladies, visits Christ's Hospitall, talks with My Lady, drinks at the Mitre, and reports on family and financial matters.

The Diarist's Wife
The wife of the diary writer, who receives £4 from the diarist to spend on lace and other items for herself.<SEP>The wife of the diarist; she tells him about the robbery and accompanies him to Whitehall.<SEP>The wife of the Diarist, reported to be in good health.

The Lord
A nobleman at whose lodgings in Westminster the diarist dines with Ned Dickering.

Ned Dickering
A man who dines with the diarist and the Lord at the Lord's lodgings in Westminster.

Sir William Pen
A companion of the diarist who joins in playing bowls at Sir R. Slingsby's alley, walks home with the diarist, and spends the evening on the garden leads talking, singing, and drinking claret.<SEP>One of the two "Sir Williams" who traveled by coach to Walthamstow; appears with Sir W. Batten in the party.

Sir R. Slingsby
A man in whose alley the diarist and Sir William Pen play bowls and afterward drink and talk.<SEP>A man The Narrator visited after supper; with his brother and The Narrator, he went to My Lord's residence at The Wardrobe.<SEP>Person at whose lodgings the Narrator sleeps while the Narrator's house is being painted and whitened.<SEP>A knight who, with the Narrator, went to inspect Sir R. Ford's house before sitting down at the office.

Captain Lambert
An officer who has just been made captain of the ship Norwich, accompanies the diarist by water to Greenwich, and later goes with the diarist to Bridewell.<SEP>A host and acquaintance who entertained the diarist and his wife at his house.

Mr. Holland
A man in Bridewell to whom the diarist owes money and whose house the diarist and Captain Lambert visit.<SEP>Mr. Holland is a man living in Bridewell whom the narrator visited; the narrator owed him money and his wife and mother were present.

Mrs. Holland
The wife of Mr. Holland, described as a plain dowdy, who is paid the money owed by the diarist to her husband.<SEP>Mrs. Holland is Mr. Holland's wife; she received the money that the narrator owed to her husband.

Norwich
A ship of which Captain Lambert has been made captain.

Wardrobe
A place visited by the diarist on the way to Whitehall and Westminster.<SEP>The Wardrobe is the place where the narrator dined with My Lady and where Mr. Townsend is connected to a mystery.<SEP>Building to which the Narrator returns; My Lord is found there before going to Trinity House, and My Lady and the children dine there with the Narrator.<SEP>The place where the narrator goes and dines with My Lady.

Greenwich
A place reached by water where the diarist and Captain Lambert eat, drink, and hear music at the Globe.<SEP>A place on the Thames where the King's yacht is seen.

The Globe
A place in Greenwich where the diarist and Captain Lambert go to eat, drink, and hear music, and where a woman with a rod keeps time to the music.<SEP>The theatre where the 1608 comedy was acted.

Bridewell
A place visited by the diarist and Captain Lambert in order to go to Mr. Holland's house.<SEP>Bridewell is the location of Mr. Holland's house, where the narrator and the Captain went.

Flageolette
A musical instrument that the diarist takes in hot weather and plays upon the garden leads.

Captain Lambert's House
The house of Captain Lambert on the water route back from Greenwich; it is described as very handsome and neat, with a fine prospect at the top.<SEP>The house belonging to Captain Lambert and Captain Lambert's Wife, visited by the diarist and the diarist's wife, containing a turret-garden and a harpsicon, and where a little witty child was kept.

The Garden Leads
The lead-covered area adjoining the garden where the diarist plays the flageolette and where the diarist and Sir William Pen stay talking and singing in the evening.

Captain
The Captain is a man who accompanied the narrator to Bridewell at the start of the passage.

My Lady at Wardrobe
My Lady at Wardrobe is the woman who dined with the narrator at the Wardrobe and treated the narrator kindly.

Sir William Batten
Sir William Batten is a man who came from Chatham with My Lady Batten and whose house the narrator visited.

My Lady Batten
My Lady Batten is the woman who came from Chatham with Sir William Batten and was much troubled with toothache.<SEP>Wife of Sir W. Batten; attended the burial of Sir John Lawson's daughter and received funeral rings.<SEP>The wife of Sir W. Batten, present at the Theatre with Sir W. Pen.<SEP>A woman who, with her daughter, looks askew at the Narrator’s wife because the wife does not seek their acquaintance.

Mr. Shepley
Mr. Shepley is a man who dined with the narrator at the Cook's.<SEP>Companion who goes out with the Narrator to drink Lambeth ale at a nearby house.

Mr. Rawlinson
Mr. Rawlinson is a man from whom the narrator sought advice about answering Uncle Robert's letter.<SEP>Host at whose house My Father, the Narrator, and relatives meet and read The Will.

Uncle Robert
Uncle Robert is the narrator's uncle who sent the narrator a letter offering a purchase of land adjacent to Uncle Robert's own lands.<SEP>The diarist's uncle, who had a dizzy spell and whose illness prompted My Father to visit him and look after his business.<SEP>Brother of Samuel Pepys's father, living at Brampton, whose condition was uncertain when his brother came to visit him.<SEP>An uncle of the narrator; mentioned in relation to the narrator's father's financial situation.

Narrator's Wife
The Narrator's Wife is the wife of the first-person narrator, frequently appearing alongside him in domestic, social, and leisure contexts. She walks with him on the leads before they go to bed, receives money from him for lace and other items, and gives linen to the Narrator. Her health is sometimes delicate: on one occasion she is found not sick but out of order, and one of her petticoats was later made into a faced white coat.

She actively shares in the Narrator's social life. She dines at home with him, attends church with him, and joins him in outings, including going by coach to dinner at Thos Pepys's and then to the theatre. She also dines at the Wardrobe, goes to Drury Lane, meets a son of Lord Somersett, and enjoys seeing the royal party at the Theatre. She hosts visitors, visits Sir W. Pen's daughter, and is criticized by Lady Batten and her daughter. She also requests the Narrator to help Balty, showing her involvement in family and patronage matters.

Chatham
Chatham is the place from which Sir William Batten and My Lady Batten came.

Cook's
Cook's is an eating-house where the narrator dined with Mr. Shepley and Mr. Creed.

Theatre
The Theatre is the playhouse where the narrator saw Bartholomew Faire performed.<SEP>The place to which the narrator and wife went after dinner to see a play.

Tobacco Shop
The Tobacco Shop under Temple Bar gate is where the narrator and Mr. Creed went up and drank Lambeth ale.

Bartholomew Faire
Bartholomew Faire is a play acted at the Theatre, described by the narrator as admirable but too profane and abusive.

Uncle Robert's Letter
Uncle Robert's Letter is a letter containing an offer to the narrator to purchase land adjoining Uncle Robert's own lands.

Mr. Holland's Mother
Mr. Holland's mother was present at Mr. Holland's house in Bridewell while the narrator visited.

Two Young Gentlewomen
Two unnamed young gentlewomen came to see Mr. Holland; one of them could play the violin fairly well.

Temple Bar Gate
A London landmark gate under which the tobacco shop visited by the narrator and Mr. Creed was located.

My Wife
Wife of The Diarist. My Wife wears a black silk gown laced with black gimp lace and accompanies The Diarist to My Lady's residence at The Wardrobe.<SEP>The Narrator's wife, whom the Narrator met at The Wardrobe.

Narrator's Father
Narrator's Father is the father of the narrator and of Tom, and is described as the owner of a trade that has now passed to Tom. He is an active presence in family and social life, dining at the narrator's house, being visited by the narrator for supper on another occasion, and going with the narrator to the Bear Tavern. The narrator also writes to him when no word has arrived, and he is said to be staying alone at Brampton in good health. While at Brampton, he reads the uncle's will in the garden and, with the narrator, looks over the uncle's papers and clothes. He walks with his son through Holborn and plans to go to Brampton, and he is the intended recipient of money that the narrator wishes to lay out.

His involvement extends to business and household matters. He participates in deciding to buy scarlet, purple, black cloth, and linen. He is also involved in arrangements and the dispute concerning Pall, in settling accounts, and in visits to relatives. On one occasion he is present at an alehouse with Uncle Fenner, after which he dismisses the servant Ned.

The father also plays a role in discussions about Tom's marriage. He dines at the narrator's house and later meets Mr. Evans at an alehouse to discuss the proposed marriage for Tom, which is also described as a match between Tom and the broker's daughter. These discussions are part of his broader engagement with the family’s affairs and Tom’s future.

Mr. Pierce
Acquaintance of The Diarist near Whitehall. Mr. Pierce joins The Diarist and Mr. Symons at the Swan Tavern.

Mr. Symons
Dancing master. Mr. Symons goes to sea with My Lord and goes with Mr. Pierce and The Diarist to the Swan Tavern.

Dean Fuller
Dean who meets The Diarist at Whitehall. Dean Fuller discusses the Bishop of Galloway's practice of admitting people into orders.<SEP>A dean whom Pepys took along when going to dine with My Lady at the Wardrobe.<SEP>A dean whom The Diarist took along when going to dine with My Lady.<SEP>A visitor who comes to the diary narrator's house to see the narrator just after the narrator's return and accompanies the narrator to My Lady's house.

Bishop of Galloway
Bishop criticized by Dean Fuller for taking liberty in admitting anyone into orders, including Roundtree.

Roundtree
Simple mechanic formerly in the fleet. Roundtree is admitted into orders by the Bishop of Galloway.

W. Howe
Companion who joins The Diarist at Whitehall, goes to The Wardrobe, and sings at Jane Shore's Tower.<SEP>Person who was to bring My Lord's things; his late arrival made My Lord angry, and The Narrator later takes leave of him.

Charles II
King of England. Charles II makes My Lord an ambassador and is married to Katherine of Braganza.<SEP>King who married Katherine of Braganza on May 21, 1662; after the death of Charles II, Katherine lived at Somerset House and later returned to Portugal.

Katherine of Braganza
Queen brought over by My Lord. Katherine of Braganza is the daughter of John IV of Portugal and the wife of Charles II.<SEP>Daughter of John IV of Portugal, born 1638; married Charles II on May 21, 1662; after the death of Charles II lived at Somerset House; returned to Portugal and became Regent of Portugal in 1704; died December 31, 1705.

John IV of Portugal
King of Portugal and father of Katherine of Braganza.

Swan Tavern
Drinking establishment visited by The Diarist, Mr. Pierce, and Mr. Symons.

Worcester House
House by the river where Dean Fuller is landed from a sculler.<SEP>House where several Lords met in Council and where the King arrived while Pepys waited.

Jane Shore's Tower
Tower associated with The Wardrobe. The Diarist and W. Howe go up there and sing.

Black Silk Gown
Gown owned by My Wife. My Wife wears it after it is laced all over with black gimp lace.

Black Gimp Lace
Black lace trimming that laces My Wife's black silk gown all over.

Mr. Pierce's Wife
Wife of Mr. Pierce. The Diarist sat with Mr. Pierce's Wife for a good while at Mr. Pierce's residence; she is described as continuing very pretty.

Don Pedro
Brother of Katherine of Braganza; in 1704 Don Pedro retired, after which Katherine became Regent of Portugal.

Portugal
Country to which Katherine of Braganza returned after the death of Charles II and where Katherine became Regent in 1704.<SEP>The country for which Lord Sandwich's preparations required 5,000 pounds.<SEP>The country to which Capt. Isham is about to make a voyage.<SEP>The destination of Mr Fanshaw and Captain Isham's voyage and the country for which Lord Sandwich's departure was being prepared.

Somerset House
London residence where Katherine of Braganza lived for some time after the death of Charles II.

Algier
North African city, written as Algier, where My Lord is to go to settle business and put the fleet in order.

Lisbone
Portuguese port city, written as Lisbone, to which My Lord is to return with three ships to meet the fleet following My Lord.

Lord Chancellor
Official from whom the Narrator receives orders during My Lord's absence.<SEP>Lord Chancellor is a high official who is envied and undermined by the Duke of Buckingham and the Lord of Bristoll; the King relies on the Lord Chancellor for policy and service.

Mr. Edward Montagu
Person from whom the Narrator receives orders during My Lord's absence as to the great preparation.<SEP>A man found by the narrator at My Lord's Whitehall residence; he comes with his family to stay during My Lord's absence.<SEP>Man in Westminster visited by the diarist about business concerning My Lord.<SEP>Man disposing of L5000 for Lord Sandwich's departure; the narrator and Lady Sandwich feared Mr Edward Montagu would not act to Lord Sandwich's honour or profit.

Trinity House
Organization that chooses a Master; My Lord is chosen Master of Trinity House and dines there on that day.

Office
Administrative office at which the Narrator works and where Sir G. Carteret joins the Narrator. The Office has no money, its credit is low, and sellers will not supply without personal security.<SEP>A place the narrator goes to after visiting the painters.<SEP>A workplace where the Diarist spent the whole afternoon and enjoyed talking with persons of quality and being in command.<SEP>The office where the Narrator and colleagues are; quiet but lacking money, with bills sold at a loss and a plan to add a house.

Sir G. Carteret
Person at the Office with the Narrator; Sir G. Carteret agrees with the Narrator on a letter to the Duke of York about the Office's lack of money.<SEP>A man who had invited some officers to dinner at Deptford but did not send for the narrator to go with them.

Duke of York
Person to whom a letter from the Office is to be sent describing the Office's need for money.<SEP>Royal person who sent an order to Samuel Pepys to give an account of why the ships had not been sent out and who received the account at Whitehall.<SEP>A person whom the Narrator, Sir W. Batten, and Sir W. Pen wait upon to give an account of the Navy's condition.<SEP>The royal duke who receives an account of the Navy's lack of money and says he will speak to the King and Council about it.

Walden
Parliament-man for Huntingdon and companion of the Narrator on the outing to drink Lambeth ale.

Rolt
Companion of the Narrator on the outing to drink Lambeth ale.

Mackworth
Companion of the Narrator on the outing to drink Lambeth ale.

Alderman Backwell
Alderman and companion of the Narrator on the outing to drink Lambeth ale.<SEP>Alderman whose premises The Narrator visits and who is designated to pay the imprest money ordered for The Narrator.<SEP>The alderman from whose premises the narrator takes L300.

Fleet
Naval fleet involved in My Lord's expedition; My Lord is to put the fleet in order at Algier, and a following fleet is to reach My Lord at Lisbone.

My Lady's Children
Unnamed children of My Lady's household at the Wardrobe who dined by themselves with the Narrator, were very merry, and were very fond of the Narrator.

Huntingdon
Town and parliamentary constituency that Walden serves as Parliament-man.<SEP>Huntingdon is a town to which the narrator travels to meet Sir Robert Bernard, where several social and business meetings take place.<SEP>A town where the Assizes also begin.<SEP>Town mentioned together with Cambridge at the beginning of the passage in connection with Samuel Pepys's journey to meet Roger Pepys.<SEP>A town that The Narrator rides to; The Narrator waits there, later returns, and drinks there with Thomas Trice and Mr. Phillips.

Whitehall
Whitehall is a royal and governmental precinct in London, closely associated with the court and official business. It appears as the site of My Lord’s house or residence, where the diarist or narrator sought My Lord, and also as a place the narrator went to and later met My Lord. Access was often by water: Whitehall was the destination of My Lord’s barge, and the narrator and his wife travelled there by water; on another occasion the narrator went with My Lord by barge, and My Lord took leave of the King at Whitehall. At that royal location, the Duke of York, the King, and the Portuguese Ambassador were present.

In the diary’s itinerary, Whitehall fits between the Wardrobe and Westminster: the narrator visited it on the 5th after going to the Wardrobe and before proceeding to Westminster. While at Whitehall, the diarist walked about, met Mr. Pierce and Dean Fuller, and was joined by W. Howe. He also went there early one morning, but the Lord Privy Seal did not come that morning. On the 15th, Whitehall was a royal and government location where the diarist walked about. On another visit, the narrator stayed at Whitehall until past three o’clock, and while there Mr. Moore gave him news of Lady Sandwich. Thus, Whitehall serves in the account as both a court and government setting for official encounters and as a place connected to My Lord’s residence, personal meetings, and the exchange of news.

Captain Rolt
A captain who accompanied The Narrator and Ferrers to Lambeth and drank with them at the Three Mariners.<SEP>Friend aboard the Dutch Yacht from whom The Narrator takes leave.

Ferrers
A companion who accompanied The Narrator and Captain Rolt to Lambeth and drank with them at the Three Mariners.

Captain Bun
A boat captain found going down the river; he gave The Narrator's party passage in his boat and landed some passengers at Westminster and The Narrator at The Bridge.

The Duke
The noble recipient of a letter The Narrator wrote at home.<SEP>The person whose letter complained about the delay in getting ships ready.

Thomas Greenfield
Preacher of Lincoln's Inn who preached a sermon before The Commons.

The Bishops
The bishops who were not ready to keep the fast for foul weather before fair weather came, so the day was kept between a fast and a feast.

His Majesty
The monarch by whose authority A Form of Prayer was set forth.

The Lords
The assembly of peers who taxed themselves for the poor, with an earl paying 30 shillings and a baron 20 shillings.<SEP>Group of noblemen who taxed themselves for the poor.

The Commons
The assembly before whom Thomas Greenfield preached a sermon.

High Court of Parliament
The Parliament then assembled, for which A Form of Prayer besought a blessing.

Lincoln's Inn
The institution of which Thomas Greenfield was preacher.

Lambeth
A district across the river from Westminster where The Narrator, Captain Rolt, and Ferrers went to drink at the Three Mariners.

Three Mariners
An alehouse in Lambeth noted for its ale where the party drank a morning draft.

The Bridge
A riverside bridge where Captain Bun landed The Narrator.

Barbary
The region where My Lord planned to give cloth as presents among the Turks.

A Form of Prayer
A prayer document published for use in London on the 12th and in the country on the 19th of June; set forth by His Majesty's authority; it contained prayers against sicknesses, dearth, and scarcity, thanksgiving for fair weather, and a blessing on Parliament.

General Fast
A special appointed fasting day on 12 and 19 June to avert feared sicknesses, dearth, and scarcity after immoderate rain and waters, and to give thanks for the blessed change of weather.

The Office
The Office was the workplace of the diarist/Narrator, Samuel Pepys, where he went to sit and do business. He attended The Office at various times of day: after dinner in the evening, during the afternoon after visits, at the beginning of the day, and for whole mornings, including the whole morning on the 31st and again on August 2nd. On one occasion he was called there while guests were present and stayed only briefly before returning home. On another, he went there after coming home by water and remained until night after dining. He also spent an afternoon there in command, talking with people of quality.

The Office was a place where he and his colleagues resumed morning sittings and conducted business, sometimes meeting there about the business of Tangier. A particular route shows him going to The Office after Duck Lane and before going to Sir W. Batten’s house. Sir R. Ford’s house was added, or might be added, as additional quarters for The Office. While at The Office one morning, news of a dying man was brought to him, and he returned there after visiting the man. On another occasion, he spent the morning there while the office clerks attended Tom Whitton’s burial.

The Poor
People for whose benefit The Lords taxed themselves, with an earl paying 30 shillings and a baron 20 shillings.<SEP>People in poverty mentioned as the intended beneficiaries of a tax the Lords imposed on themselves.

The Turks
People among whom My Lord planned to distribute cloth presents in Barbary.

Sir R. Slingsby's Brother
Unnamed brother of Sir R. Slingsby who went with Sir R. Slingsby and The Narrator to My Lord's residence at The Wardrobe.

Sir Robert Slingsby
Also referred to as Sir R. Slingsby and Sir Robert; joins The Narrator at the Wardrobe, takes leave of My Lord, and is thanked by My Lord for kindness to The Narrator.

Mr. Shaw
Person encountered at Alderman Backwell's premises who offers L300 in connection with a cloth purchase that My Lord may approve.

Captain Ferrers
Person who accompanies The Narrator into a wherry after the yachting party departs.<SEP>The captain whose lady or wife was part of the merry company that ate a good venison pasty.<SEP>Captain Ferrers is the man whose lady was mentioned among the friends present at the Wardrobe for Lord Of Sandwich's birthday.<SEP>A captain who was taken by the narrator with two young gentlemen and two ladies to the Theatre.<SEP>A captain who accompanies the diarist to the Theatre to see The Alchymist.<SEP>A man who accompanied the narrator to the Opera, saw The Witts, and drank at the Devil Tavern.

The Theatre
The Theatre is a playhouse attended by the diarist Samuel Pepys and his associates. It staged a variety of plays, including *Harry the 4th*, *The Alchymist*, *Claracilla*, *Brenoralt*, *The Jovial Crew* (also written as “The Joviall Crew”), and *Antipodes*. Pepys visited on several occasions, sometimes in the afternoon, and once carried his own party to see a performance there. He saw *Claracilla* in the afternoon of the 4th and noted that the theatre had become empty since the Opera began. He also watched *Brenoralt* while sitting before Mrs. Palmer, and met Mr. Bostock when seeing *Antipodes*.

Other attendees included Sir W. Pen and My Lady Batten, who were present for a performance of *The Alchymist* and also at an afternoon visit. Mr. Moore accompanied Pepys to see *The Jovial Crew*, at which the royal party was present. The theatre thus served not only as a venue for dramatic performances, but as a regular site of social engagement among Pepys’s circle.

Dutch Yacht
Vessel at Deptford on which My Lord's party sails; My Lord has five guns fired from it as The Narrator leaves.

Erith
A place on the river from which some of the party sail away.<SEP>Place from which the yacht sails after The Narrator leaves the party.

The Downs
A sea area where those sailing from Erith hope to arrive early the next day.<SEP>Anchorage where the party hopes to arrive the following day.

Sir Robert Slingsby's Brother
The unnamed brother of Sir Robert Slingsby who accompanied Sir Robert Slingsby and The Narrator to My Lord's residence at The Wardrobe.

The Narrator's Wife
The wife of The Narrator; one of The Narrator's Wife's petticoats was used to make a coat that The Narrator wore on the 13th.<SEP>The Narrator's Wife is the woman who met the Narrator at the Wardrobe on Lord of Sandwich's birthday.<SEP>The narrator's wife, who hired the chambermaid and informed the narrator about Mrs. Hater's labor.<SEP>The wife of the narrator who went with Mr. Hater because his wife was in labour.<SEP>Wife of the narrator; accompanies Lady Sandwich's children by coach, dines at the narrator's father's house, and visits Mrs. Cordery.<SEP>Wife of the narrator; rides by coach with the narrator to Uncle Fenner's house.

My Father
The narrator's father, who buys cloth to send to My Lord and discusses the cloth business with the narrator.<SEP>The diarist's father, who looked for The Diarist about special business, went with him to Mr. Starling's for a morning drink, and went to Uncle Robert because Uncle Robert was ill.<SEP>Father of the Narrator; arranges papers before removal, goes to Mr. Rawlinson's, and is visited by Mrs. Cordery.

Young Poole
A younger man named Poole who takes the narrator aboard The Charity and gives him wine there.

Mr. Kennersley
A young man who is part of the company that goes ashore at Woolwich with the narrator.

Mr. Falconer
A man with whom the narrator's party goes home and who gives them cherries and good wine.

King's Yacht
The royal vessel at Greenwich in which The King is present.<SEP>The royal yacht whose purser is to provide stowage; connected with the Duke of York's planned travel.

The Charity
A boat or ship aboard which Young Poole takes the narrator and gives him wine.

Triangle Virginall
A musical instrument that is My Lord's property and is sent to the narrator's house by My Lord's order.

Cloth
Material that My Father is ordered to buy for the purpose of sending it to My Lord.

The Tower
A landmark near which the narrator wakes on the wherry and parts from Captain Poole.

Jamaica
The place associated with Captain Poole.

Purser of the King's Yacht
The purser who arrives seeking victuals and promises stowage for the narrator's goods.

Duke Of York
A duke who was expected to make a journey; the narrator later hears that the duke went during the night.

Will
The narrator's servant; sent to fetch goods and later sent about town to obtain information.<SEP>The Diarist's servant, who lost a clock and a tankard.

Mr. Ch. Carter
An old friend of the narrator who visits the narrator and walks with the narrator to Westminster.

The Spanish Gypsey
A play read by the narrator and considered by the narrator to be not very good despite being much commended.

Margate Hoy
A hired vessel that takes the narrator's goods on board during the night to carry them toward the Downs.

Carrier
A carrier whose goods service is used to bring items to the narrator's house and considered for sending them to Deal.

Painters
Workmen employed by the narrator, currently painting the narrator's stairs.<SEP>The workmen employed by the diarist to paint and finish his stairs.

Deal
A destination considered for sending the goods by carrier on Wednesday.

Downs
The anchorage where the narrator hopes the goods will arrive the following night.

Sir W. Pen's House
The house of Sir W. Pen where the narrator and others sit drinking until late.<SEP>The house of Sir W. Pen, where the diarist and others sat and drank until 11 o'clock at night.

Diarist
The first-person speaker in the diary extract, who manages household work, visits acquaintances and relatives, and records daily events.<SEP>The unnamed writer of the diary excerpt, referred to as "I"; records personal activities, family encounters, and political hearsay.

Diarist's Wife
The wife of the diarist, who accompanies him by water to Captain Lambert's house.<SEP>Wife of the diarist; attended the burial of Sir John Lawson's daughter and received funeral rings.<SEP>Wife of the Diarist; present at the Diarist's mother's house with Aunt Bell and Mrs. Ramsey.

Lady of the Wardrobe
A lady associated with the Wardrobe with whom the diarist dined.

Captain Lambert's Wife
The wife of Captain Lambert, who made fine needleworks and played the harpsicon.

data.entity_name: Kept Little Girl at Captain Lambert's House
data.content:
Kept Little Girl at Captain Lambert's House
A little child kept at Captain Lambert's house who cried when the diarist and his wife departed.

Jack Cole
An old school friend of the diarist who visited him and stayed for a good while.

Diarist's Father
The diarist's father, met by the diarist on the way to his house and joined for a morning drink at the Samson.<SEP>Father of the diarist; had gone to Brampton and wrote a letter describing the uncle's illness.<SEP>Father of the Diarist; subject of Uncle Wight's discontent and recipient of a letter from the Diarist.

Westminster Hall
A hall the diarist visited with Mr. Moore during term time.<SEP>Hall in Westminster where the diarist walked during term time and spoke with Roger Pepys.<SEP>The hall in Westminster where the narrator talked with Mrs. Michell.<SEP>The hall at Westminster where the diarist stayed talking with Mrs. Michell.<SEP>Westminster Hall is the hall in Westminster where Parliament's adjournment was expected to be announced and where the Narrator spoke with Mr. George Montagu in the lobby.<SEP>A hall The Narrator visits where The King is expected to come and adjourn Parliament.

The Exchange
A building the diarist went to at night to meet Uncle Wight.<SEP>The place over against which the ordinary stood.<SEP>A place Samuel Pepys visits at night before meeting Uncle Wight at the Mitre.<SEP>A place visited by the Diarist at noon, where he met Uncle Wight.<SEP>A place where bills related to the Navy were offered for sale.<SEP>The London financial venue where the Navy's bills are offered for sale at 20 in the 100 loss.<SEP>The building where the Narrator meets Dr. Williams by appointment.

Westminster
Westminster, a location in London, appears in the diary of Samuel Pepys as both a site of business and social activity. Pepys visited Westminster on multiple occasions to conduct several items of business, including once before dining at the Wardrobe and again on the 23rd after visiting Sir W. Pen and Batten. It was the location of Mr. Montagu’s chamber. The diarist also went to Westminster by accompanying Mr. Ch. Carter before the two parted ways.

Westminster was also a setting for social encounters and travel. Pepys went there to dine with the Lord, who had lodgings in the area, and with Ned Dickering. He walked to Westminster together with Mr. Marsh and Mr. Marsh’s wife. Westminster was accessible from Whitehall via a passage; the narrator traveled from Whitehall to Westminster at the end of that passage. Additionally, Westminster lay on the river, where Captain Bun landed some of the boat’s passengers.

Samson in Paul's Churchyard
A place, apparently an inn or tavern in Paul's Churchyard, where the diarist and his father drank a morning draft.

Stairs of the Diarist's House
The stairway at the diarist's home that was painted and finished by the painters.

Turret-Garden at Captain Lambert's
A garden in a turret at Captain Lambert's house where the diarist took great pleasure.

Needleworks by Captain Lambert's Wife
Fine needlework pieces created by Captain Lambert's wife, admired by the diarist.

Harpsicon at Captain Lambert's House
A harpsichord at Captain Lambert's house on which Captain Lambert's wife made music.

Diarist's House
The home of the diarist, where painters and workmen painted and finished the stairs and where the diarist experienced dirt and trouble during the work.

Diary Narrator
The first-person speaker of the diary entry who meets relatives, dines with acquaintances, attends a play, and walks to entertainment grounds over three days.<SEP>The person who wrote the diary account; rides by horse from Baldwick toward London and is later expected at the Privy Seal during the narrator's month of duty.

Diary Narrator's Father
Father of the narrator; the narrator meets the father in the morning and the two drink together at the Samson before parting.<SEP>Father of the diary narrator; lives at the home to which the narrator returns and discerns that the narrator had been drinking.

Diary Narrator's Wife
Wife of the narrator; reported unwell on Sunday, so the wife remains away from church.

Mr. Norbury
Guest at Uncle Wight's dinner; discusses with the narrator the wife's house and land at Brampton.

Mr. Norbury's Wife
Wife of Mr. Norbury; owner of the house and land at Brampton considered by the narrator as a possible purchase.

Lady Crew
Wife of Lord Crew; joins Lord Crew in making much of the narrator at dinner.

Little Luellin
Acquaintance who, with Blirton, takes the narrator to Mr. Hodges's house in Lincoln's Inn Fields.

Blirton
Acquaintance who, with Little Luellin, takes the narrator to Mr. Hodges's house in Lincoln's Inn Fields.

Mr. Hodges
Friend of Little Luellin and Blirton in Lincoln's Inn Fields; host of the drinking visit there.

Captain Allen
A visitor who came to Pepys with his daughter Rebecca and Mr. Hempson.<SEP>Guest at Sir W. Batten's Sunday dinner and father of Rebecca Allen.

Rebecca Allen
Captain Allen's daughter, who came with Captain Allen to visit Pepys.<SEP>Daughter of Captain Allen; present at Sir W. Batten's Sunday dinner.

Mr. Hempson
A visitor who came with Captain Allen to visit Pepys.<SEP>Guest at Sir W. Batten's Sunday dinner, accompanied by Mrs. Hempson.

Mrs. Hempson
Wife of Mr. Hempson; guest at Sir W. Batten's Sunday dinner.

Mrs. Frances Butler
Woman seen at Graye's Inn Walks; sister of Monsieur L'Impertinent and described as the greatest beauty among the ladies there.

Monsieur L'Impertinent
The brother of Frances Butler.<SEP>Brother of Mrs. Frances Butler; mentioned by that name in the diary entry.

Ben Jonson
Playwright identified in a note as the author of the comedy The Alchymist.<SEP>Playwright credited as the author of The Alchymist.

The Samson in Paul's Churchyard
House in Paul's Churchyard where the narrator and the narrator's father drink a morning draft and eat gammon.

Exchequer
Office that the narrator visits on business and where the narrator meets Uncle Wight.

Lincoln's Inn Fields
Area where Mr. Hodges lives and where the narrator goes with Little Luellin and Blirton.

Graye's Inn Walks
Promenade with gallants and ladies where the narrator walks with the young company and sees Mrs. Frances Butler.<SEP>The walks where the narrator met Ned Pickering.

Islington
A place visited by Pepys, where Pepys entertained companions at the great house.<SEP>Place to which the narrator and the young company travel from Graye's Inn Walks.

The Great House at Islington
Large house in Islington where the narrator entertains the young company.

The Alchymist
Comedy by Ben Jonson that the narrator goes to see at the Theatre and calls an incomparable play.<SEP>A play performed at the Theatre which the diarist and Captain Ferrers witness.<SEP>Comedy written by Ben Jonson.

Green Say
Green woollen cloth bought by the narrator for curtains in the parlour.

Narrator's Aunt
Aunt of the narrator and wife of Uncle Wight; she was out of town when the narrator dined at Uncle Wight's house.<SEP>Aunt of the narrator; found in bed in a very unpleasant state, and the aunt's base, ugly humours troubled the narrator.

Young Company
Group of younger companions who went with the narrator after church to Graye's Inn Walks and from there to Islington, where the narrator entertained them at the great house.

Pepys
The diary narrator identified as Pepys by the editorial note, who visits places, settles accounts, receives visitors, and begins singing lessons.<SEP>Diary writer who narrates the passage. Pepys records waiting at Worcester House, traveling to Chelsy with Mr. Moore, meeting Mr. Marsh, and noting payments to the Chancellor.

Frances Butler
A woman described as the greatest beauty and as the sister of Monsieur L'Impertinent.<SEP>One of the two fair Butlers seen at Clerkenwell Church; identified in the text's parenthetical note as Mrs. Frances Butler.

Uncle Wight
Uncle Wight is a relative—specifically an uncle—of the diarist Samuel Pepys, appearing in Pepys’s diary as a recurring family figure. In one account, he was out of town, which led Pepys to seek advice from Mr. Rawlinson instead; in another, he was not at home when Pepys called at his house.

Uncle Wight was involved in family business and social visits. Pepys visited him at the Exchange to discuss a purchase at Brampton, and on another occasion encountered him at the Exchange, where Uncle Wight was discontented with Pepys’s father. He also met Pepys at the Exchequer and brought him home for dinner. He went with Pepys to the Mitre, where he was upset that Pepys’s father had not told him about the Brampton trip, and where he was informed of Robert Pepys’s death. Later, Pepys and his father found Uncle Wight at a Coffee House, and he agreed to the meeting for the reading of a will.

In further family gatherings, Uncle Wight went out with Pepys and Pepys’s father to an alehouse because the house was too hot, and he also received a visit and supper from them. Overall, Uncle Wight appears as an uncle whose interactions with Pepys were marked by family news, business discussions concerning Brampton, and shared meals or meetings at various London locations.

Kate Joyce
A person whose child had a christening that Pall attended.

Kate Joyce's Child's Christening
The christening of Kate Joyce's child, attended by Pall.

Pepys's Father
Pepys's father, who inspected Pepys's finished house and dined with Pepys and Dr. Williams.

Pepys's Wife
Pepys's wife, whose sore belly had become dangerous in the wife's opinion and who was visited by Dr. Williams.<SEP>Wife of Samuel Pepys who dined alone with him at home and felt out of order though not yet sick.

Pepys's House
Pepys's newly finished house, described as neat, which Pepys's father came to inspect.

Pepys's Father's House
The house where Pall stayed overnight after the christening.

Dr. Williams
A doctor who came to see Pepys's wife and dined at an ordinary with Pepys and Pepys's father.<SEP>A doctor whom the narrator and the narrator's father go to see but do not find at home.<SEP>A man visited by the narrator and the narrator's father; Dr. Williams signs a copy of an uncle's will and later dines with the narrator at a cook's shop.<SEP>An acquaintance who meets the Narrator at the Exchange and discusses Aunt Pepys's £200 bond.

Theodore Goodgroome
Pepys's singing-master, also called Mr. Goodgroome, who was recommended by Mr. Mage and began teaching Pepys to sing.<SEP>Singing master of Samuel Pepys who dined at Pepys's home and then joined in singing practice.<SEP>Singing master of the diarist; dined with the diarist and gave the diarist a singing lesson.

Mr. Mage
The person who recommended Theodore Goodgroome to Pepys.<SEP>A man met at the tavern near the Savoy with whom the narrator discoursed about music; Mr. Mage left after being angered by Mons. Eschar's praise of French music.

John Goodgroome
A probable relative of Theodore Goodgroome and a Gentleman of the Chapel Royal.

Chapel Royal
The royal chapel of which John Goodgroome was a Gentleman.

La cruda la bella
The first song used by Theodore Goodgroome when teaching Pepys to sing.

Master of the House
The person who managed the ordinary where Pepys and his companions dined and who set down every item at an excessively high price when the reckoning was brought.

The Ordinary
An eating house over against the Exchange where Pepys, Pepys's father, and Dr. Williams dined and wrangled with the master of the house.

The Two Drapers
The two unnamed cloth dealers with whom Pepys and Tom made even for cloths sent to sea.

Both Sir Williams
The two men titled Sir William who arrived at Pepys's house in the afternoon and sat with Pepys until late.

The Great House
The large house in Islington where Pepys entertained his companions.

My Aunt
The diarist's aunt, who wrote to My Father that Uncle Robert was dizzy and needed My Father's help.

Mr. Starling
A person at whose house or establishment The Diarist and My Father drank a morning draft.

Mrs. Rebecca Allen
A woman who was part of the two-coach party that went to see Bartholomew Fayre.

Mrs. Thompson
A woman who was part of the two-coach party that went to see Bartholomew Fayre.

Mr. Holden
A person who sent The Diarist a Bever.

Bartholomew Fayre
A play seen by The Diarist and companions, which was acted very well.

Bever
A beaver headpiece sent by Mr. Holden to The Diarist, costing L4 5s.

Moorefields
An area in London where Samuel Pepys and Sir W. Pen walked and watched wrestling between northern and western countrymen.

The Bell at the Maypole
A tavern in the Strand where Samuel Pepys met by appointment Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, Hartlibb, and Mr. Kipps.

Mr. Chetwind
A friend from Samuel Pepys's old club; he became fat and sallow from chewing tobacco and praised Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity.

Gregory
A friend from Samuel Pepys's old club who met Pepys at the Bell.

Hartlibb
A friend from Samuel Pepys's old club who met Pepys at the Bell.

Mr. Kipps
A friend who joined Samuel Pepys and the old club members at the Bell.

Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity
A book commended by Mr. Chetwind as the best book and the one that made him a Christian; Samuel Pepys decided to buy it.<SEP>A theological work given to the narrator by Mr. Moore; read by the narrator at night.

The Nursery
A room in Samuel Pepys's house where his bed was set up and where he slept, much to his pleasure.

St. Olave Hart Street
A church in London mentioned in an editorial note as the site where collections recorded in an old account-book were made.

St. Dunstan in the West
A parish in London whose inhabitants received collections toward their loss by fire, as recorded in the old account-book.<SEP>A parish or church mentioned in a note about church briefs; a brief was collected towards the parish's losses by fire, with the contribution amounting to 20s. 8d.

Old MS. Account-Book
A manuscript account-book of collections in St. Olave Hart Street church, beginning in 1642, that records money gathered for inhabitants of St. Dunstan in the West.

Trade of Briefs
The recurring Sunday practice of charitable appeals or collections referred to by Samuel Pepys; he observed that it had become so constant that he and his companions resolved to give no more to such briefs.

The Queen
Royal woman with whom the Portuguese Ambassador was going to conclude arrangements before she was sent over.

Portuguese Ambassador
Diplomat who came to Whitehall to take leave of the King and was to finalize matters with the Queen.

Samuel Pepys's Father
Father of Samuel Pepys who travelled to Brampton to see his brother Robert, not knowing whether Robert was dead or alive.<SEP>Father of Samuel Pepys, who goes to Brampton while Robert Pepys is ill; Samuel Pepys later finds the father well there.<SEP>Father of Samuel Pepys; received a letter written late at night.

Graye's Inn Walk
London walk where Samuel Pepys went alone for pleasure and saw fine ladies.

St. Olave's Church
London church at which a good sermon was heard and where church briefs had been levied.

Trillo
A singing technique or vocal ornament that Samuel Pepys hummed to himself and found improved with practice.

Chest of Drawers
Furniture item purchased by Samuel Pepys for his own chamber for 33 shillings.

Indian Gown
Gown purchased by Samuel Pepys for himself for 34 shillings.<SEP>A garment mentioned as bought for the diarist's own use, costing 34 shillings.

Church Briefs
Official church documents authorizing collections; they were levied repeatedly at St. Olave's Church and abolished in 1828.

The Ships
Vessels that had not been sent out because the wind was against them and they could not leave the river.<SEP>Ships shown by the Narrator to Lady Jem and Pall during a boat trip through the bridge.

The Wind
Contrary wind that prevented the ships from getting out of the river.

Sir Williams
Two men addressed together as "Sir Williams" who accompanied Samuel Pepys by water to Whitehall and were included in the Duke of York's order to report about the ships.

The River
The river from which the ships could not sail out because the wind was against them.

The Next Fleet
The fleet that was to be sent to the Queen and with which Samuel Pepys was preparing items to send.

Roger Pepys
Cousin of the diarist; met the diarist in Westminster Hall while going to the Parliament House.<SEP>Son of Talbot Pepys, who succeeded his father as Recorder of Cambridge in 1660 according to the editorial note.<SEP>The person The Narrator intends to meet for counsel in connection with the Assizes at Cambridge and Huntingdon.<SEP>Person whom Samuel Pepys intended to meet for counsel before setting out on horseback toward Cambridge.<SEP>A cousin of the narrator whom the narrator consults about the uncle's will; he rides with the narrator to Impington and is regarded as a sober, honorable man.<SEP>A sober relative of The Narrator with whom The Narrator discusses public matters; Roger Pepys criticizes the young men in Parliament and fears that they may cause another war.

Diarist's Uncle
Uncle of the diarist; reported by the father of the diarist to have fits of stupor, drunk-like states, and occasional speechlessness.

Parliament House
Building to which Roger Pepys was going when the diarist spoke with Roger Pepys.

Sir William Davenant
Person whose opera house staged the second part of "The Siege of Rhodes".<SEP>A person noted in the text for introducing the use of scenery; he taught Betterton how the part of Hamlet was acted by Taylor of the Blackfriars.

Sir William Davenant's Opera
Opera house attended by the diarist; had been presenting the second part of "The Siege of Rhodes" for four days.

The Siege of Rhodes
Dramatic work whose second part was acted at Sir William Davenant's Opera; the performance included the character Eunuch.

The Queen of Bohemia
Queen who attended Sir William Davenant's Opera and was waited for by the audience.

The Eunuch
Performer in "The Siege of Rhodes" at Sir William Davenant's Opera; performed so poorly that the audience hissed the performer off the stage.

Mr. Saml. Crew
Brother of My Lady; died the previous day of the spotted fever.

Spotted Fever
Disease that caused the death of Mr. Saml. Crew.

Duck Lane
Street through which the diarist passed while looking for Spanish books.

Sir John Lawson
Father of the daughter buried on that day; funeral rings were given because of that daughter.

Sir John Lawson's Daughter
Deceased daughter of Sir John Lawson; burial of the daughter was attended by My Lady Batten and the diarist's wife.

Claracilla
Play performed at The Theatre and seen by the diarist for the first time.<SEP>Play that Samuel Pepys sees at the Theatre for the first time and judges to be well acted.

Spanish Books
Books written in Spanish that the diarist looked for in Duck Lane, though none pleased him.

Sir W. Batten's House
Sir W. Batten's residence, where the diarist, the Comptroller, and Mr. Mills sat late talking and disputing.<SEP>The residence of Sir W. Batten, where Samuel Pepys and others go after the office to eat a venison pasty.

data.entity_name: The Burial of Sir John Lawson's Daughter
data.content:
The Burial of Sir John Lawson's Daughter
Burial ceremony for Sir John Lawson's daughter, attended by My Lady Batten and the diarist's wife, who received funeral rings for themselves and their husbands.

Robert Pepys
Samuel Pepys's uncle from Brampton; Robert Pepys has daily fits of stupefaction, dies, and is laid in a coffin in the hall at Brampton.

Mr. Batersby
An apothecary at the Mitre who advises that leeches and bleeding could cure Robert Pepys if Robert Pepys's stopped piles were opened.

The Opera
Opera or opera season that has recently begun and is thought by Samuel Pepys to be drawing audiences away from the Theatre.<SEP>A theatre that begins again with The Witts, performed for the first time with scenes, attended by the King, Duke, and Duchess.<SEP>Venue where Captain Ferrers and the narrator saw The Witts and where Queen of Bohemia was present.<SEP>The place to which the narrator takes the narrator's wife to see the play "The Witts."<SEP>The theatre where the Narrator sees “Hamlet, Prince of Denmark” performed.

The Mitre
A tavern where Samuel Pepys and Uncle Wight go and are merry and where Mr. Batersby is present.<SEP>A tavern where the Narrator takes Capt. Isham and gives him a glass of sack.<SEP>A tavern on Fenchurch Street where the Diarist and Mr. Moore drink wine before parting.

St. Martin's
A place in London where Samuel Pepys buys a pair of boots before beginning the ride to Brampton.

Post House
A post house from which Samuel Pepys and the messenger set out on horseback toward Brampton.

Emerods
A medical condition, also called piles, that Samuel Pepys thinks Robert Pepys may have and on which Mr. Batersby bases one possible cure.

Fits of Stupefaction
Recurring episodes of stupor that, according to what Samuel Pepys hears, Robert Pepys experiences for ten to twelve hours each day.

The Messenger
An unnamed messenger who wakes Samuel Pepys with the news of Robert Pepys's death and later rides with Samuel Pepys to Brampton.

Samuel Pepys's Father's House
The residence of Samuel Pepys's father, where Samuel Pepys calls on the 4th and hears about Robert Pepys's fits of stupefaction.

Narrator's Uncle
Deceased uncle of the narrator; the uncle's corpse was kept in a coffin at Brampton and later moved to the yard, and the uncle's will, estate, and burial were central to the events.

Tom Trice
Man who filed a caveat against the narrator and the narrator's father on behalf of Tom Trice's mother.<SEP>Tom Trice is one of the two Trices in the will dispute; his arrival is awaited before an issue can be reached, and he later takes part in the evening argument and agreement.<SEP>A man with whom the diary narrator talks at Gorum's House.<SEP>A man involved in proving an uncle's will; Tom Trice signs the copy, receives the original to prove, and takes the narrator and the narrator's father to a judge.<SEP>A man who arranges the probate of a will for the narrator.

Tom Trice's Mother
Mother of Tom Trice; the narrator's uncle gave her nothing, and Tom Trice acted on her behalf in the legal caveat.

Mr Taylor
Person who buried the narrator's uncle at the church in Brampton.

Mr Turners
Person who preached the funeral sermon at the burial of the narrator's uncle and spoke of the uncle's honesty as well known.

Uncle's Will
Legal will left by the narrator's uncle; read in the garden by the narrator and the narrator's father; gave the narrator little until the narrator's father's death and gave nothing to Tom Trice's mother.<SEP>The will of an uncle of the diarist; the diarist discusses it with relatives, and the uncle's estate is about L500.<SEP>Uncle's Will is the last will and testament of the Narrator's uncle; reading the will with Mr. Moore suggested more trouble to the Narrator.<SEP>The last will of an uncle of the narrator; it is examined before Dr. Williams and Tom Trice, a copy is signed, and the original is given to Tom Trice to prove.

Uncle's Papers
Written records left by the narrator's uncle; examined by the narrator and the narrator's father, but found in confusion and hard to understand.

Uncle's Estate
Wealth and property left by the narrator's uncle; the estate appeared to be much less valuable than expected and was a major source of trouble.

Coffin
The coffin containing the corpse of the Narrator's Uncle; it first stood on joint-stools in the hall at Brampton, then was moved to the yard overnight because the corpse began to smell.

Uncle's Burial
The burial ceremony for the Narrator's Uncle, held in the afternoon on the Lord's day at the church in Brampton, conducted by Mr Taylor, with a funeral sermon preached by Mr Turners.

Tom Trice's Caveat
A legal caveat filed by Tom Trice on behalf of Tom Trice's Mother, opposing the Narrator and the Narrator's Father in the matter of the Narrator's Uncle's estate.

Father
The father of the narrator. Father is at Brampton, walks around Portholme with the narrator, and is shielded from worry over estate troubles.<SEP>The father of The Narrator, who owns a house in London and weighs whether to profit from it or leave it to Tom.<SEP>The narrator's father, who goes with the narrator to Dr. Williams and Tom Trice for legal business and is sworn before a judge.

Mr. Philips
A man who returns home from London in the latter part of the week and is consulted for counsel about the estate.<SEP>A man involved in the argument with the narrator; later one of the witnesses to William Luffe's acknowledgment.

Robert Barnwell
A man who dines with the narrator and Father at Brampton on a Sunday.

Portholme
A field area near Brampton that the narrator and Father walk around and view; it is described as very pleasant.

Hinchingbroke
A place near Brampton visited by the narrator and Father; it is currently dirty from building work by Lord, which is expected to make it magnificent.

Lord
A nobleman whose building work at Hinchingbroke is making the place magnificent.

Cambridge
Town in which Talbot Pepys was M.P. and Recorder, and the seat of Trinity Hall.<SEP>A city to which the narrator rides early in the morning; the narrator visits Christ College and King's College Chapel there and departs at noon.<SEP>A town where the Assizes begin, and where The Narrator plans to go to meet Roger Pepys.<SEP>Town toward which Samuel Pepys set out on horseback after preparing to leave.<SEP>The city the narrator reaches; it contains Castle Hill, Trinity Hall, the Rose, and the University.

Christ College
A Cambridge college visited by the narrator, where Brother John is found in bed.

Brother John
Brother of the narrator, present at Christ College in Cambridge and found in bed at eight o'clock.

King's College Chapel
A chapel in Cambridge visited by the narrator; scholars in surplices are at service there, and Dr. Fairbrother is met there.

Dr. Fairbrother
A man met at King's College Chapel who goes with the narrator to the Rose Tavern.

Rose Tavern
A tavern in Cambridge where the narrator, Dr. Fairbrother, Mr. Turner, and Mr. Sanchy gather and are merry.

Mr. Turner's Wife
Wife of Mr. Turner; she is sent for and joins the company at the Rose Tavern.

Mr. Sanchy
A man of Magdalen who joins the narrator and others at the Rose Tavern.

Magdalen
The institution or college named in the opening phrase as the affiliation of one of the gentlemen with whom the Narrator was merry before riding toward Impington.<SEP>An institution, probably a college, with which Mr. Sanchy is associated.

Cousin Angier
A cousin of the narrator in Cambridge from whom the narrator takes leave when departing.

Estate
The property and financial affairs, called the estate, that the narrator and the family find less valuable than expected and are trying to settle.<SEP>An inheritance left to the Diarist, reported by the Diarist as L200 a year in land besides other moneys, and publicly claimed to raise the Diarist's own esteem.

Estate Papers
Documents belonging to the estate; the papers are unsorted and in confusion and vex the narrator.

Copyhold Land
Land held by copyhold tenure that is part of the estate; without the proper surrenders, the land would pass to the heir at law.

Heir at Law
The legal heir who would receive the copyhold land if the required surrenders were not made.

Copyhold Surrenders
Legal documents surrendering the copyhold land; the family missed the surrenders, so the land would not pass to them but to the heir at law.

Talbot Pepys
The narrator's old uncle, found sitting all alone at Impington, where he could hardly see but was otherwise lively. According to the editorial note, Talbot Pepys was the sixth son of John Pepys of Impington, born 1583, educated at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1605, served as M.P. for Cambridge in 1625 and Recorder of Cambridge from 1624 to 1660, and died of the plague in March 1666.

John Pepys of Impington
Father of Talbot Pepys, according to the editorial note, which identifies Talbot as the sixth son of John Pepys of Impington.

Dr. John Pepys
A relative who joined the narrator and Talbot Pepys at Impington; the narrator read over the will with him, and he gave advice on its sufficiency.

Angier
The narrator's cousin, from whom the narrator took leave before riding from Magdalen toward Impington.

Stankes
A man with whom the narrator and his family agreed to have care of their business in their absence; they considered themselves fortunate to find him as their bailiff.<SEP>Stankes is a person who, with his wife, dines with the narrator's household.

Serjeant Bernard
A person mentioned as having come home into the country on the evening of the 19th, according to what the narrator hears.

Jane Perkin
A person named in the narrator's description of his aunt's base, hypocritical tricks; the phrase "of whom we make great" is left incomplete.<SEP>Jane Perkin is a person of whom the narrator's household makes great use; she tells the narrator's household about the aunt's hypocritical tricks.

Impington
Place where the narrator found his old uncle Talbot Pepys sitting alone and where the will was read over; also the narrator's destination after leaving Magdalen.<SEP>A village to which the narrator rides with Roger Pepys and his brothers and where the narrator sleeps in the best chamber.

Gravely
Place the narrator rode to with much effort to inquire about a surrender of his uncle's estate in the hands of copyholders.<SEP>Place whose affairs Dr. John Williams knew well.

Offord
A place the narrator rode to in the course of going up and down all the family lands while overseeing business.

Sturtlow
A place the narrator rode to in the course of going up and down all the family lands while overseeing business.<SEP>The property named in the surrender made by the narrator's uncle.

Trinity Hall, Cambridge
