College at Cambridge where Talbot Pepys was educated.

Middle Temple
Inn of court at which Talbot Pepys was called to the bar in 1605.

The Will
A legal will read over by the narrator at Impington with Dr. John Pepys and Talbot Pepys; three witnesses to the will were all legatees, and Mr. Moore advised this would not invalidate it.<SEP>The Will is a legal document owned and shown by the narrator during the dispute, to be resolved in discussions with the Trice family and Sir Robert Bernard.<SEP>A legal document read at Mr. Rawlinson's during the family meeting.<SEP>A legal document whose probate is performed by Tom Trice and gives the narrator and the narrator's father satisfaction.

The Narrator's Father
The narrator's father goes to Goody Gorum's with Tom Trice and is involved in the business of settling the estate.<SEP>The parent of the Narrator, present at Brampton; the Narrator tried to seem cheerful to the Father, and the two walked about the fields talking and spent several days arranging family affairs.<SEP>The Narrator's father, who lives at Brampton, is found very well by The Narrator, discerns that The Narrator has been drinking, and later goes with The Narrator to Goody Gorum's.<SEP>The narrator's father, who returned from Brampton that day and came to the narrator's house.<SEP>Father of the narrator; dines at the narrator's home and plans to go into the country.<SEP>The father of the narrator; meets the narrator by appointment and visits Dr. Williams with the narrator.

The Narrator's Aunt
The narrator's aunt continues in base, hypocritical tricks; she is party to the will dispute and agrees to quit the house in exchange for L10.<SEP>The aunt of the Narrator, described as continuing in base, hypocritical tricks; the passage breaks off mid-sentence.<SEP>The narrator's aunt, who was to receive L10 and to quit the house under the agreement.<SEP>The Narrator's aunt, who has left the house in Brampton; The Narrator is glad of the aunt's departure though it costs the family L10.

Sir Robert Bernard
Sir Robert Bernard, also called Serjeant Bernard, is a knight living in Huntingdon who mediates discussions about a Will and hosts a dinner at his home.

Jaspar Trice
Jaspar Trice is one of the two Trices involved in the will dispute; he converses with the narrator at Sir Robert Bernard's, later drinks at Mother's, and argues in the evening.

Mr. Greene
Mr. Greene joins meetings at Goody Gorum's and the evening argument about the will.<SEP>A man involved in an argument with the narrator that resulted in an agreement.

Mr. Phillips
Mr. Phillips, also written Philips, is an acquaintance in Huntingdon with whom the narrator spends time and drinks ale, and who participates in the evening argument.<SEP>A man whom The Narrator tries to meet early and later drinks with at Huntingdon; the text spells the name as both Phillips and Philips.

Dr. Symcottes
Dr. Symcottes is an acquaintance in Huntingdon with whom the narrator spends part of the afternoon.

Mr. Vinter
Mr. Vinter is an acquaintance in Huntingdon with whom the narrator spends part of the afternoon.

Robert Ethell
Robert Ethell is an acquaintance in Huntingdon with whom the narrator spends part of the afternoon.

Mr. Davenport
Mr. Davenport is a person who joins the narrator and others to drink ale opposite the Crown.

Piggott
Piggott is a person from whom money is due to the narrator's side upon a surrender; Sir Robert Bernard says the money will go with debts to the heir at law.

Goody Gorum
Goody Gorum is a woman at whose house the narrator, Tom Trice, Jaspar Trice, Mr. Greene, and the narrator's father hold a calm discourse.<SEP>A Brampton woman whose house is visited by Thomas Trice, The Narrator, and The Narrator's father.<SEP>A person whose house or establishment is referred to as Gorum's in the diary account.

Lady Digby
Lady Digby is the wife of Sir Robert Bernard, described as a very good woman, with whom the narrator dines.

The Maid
The Maid is an unnamed maid in the narrator's household who, along with Jane Perkin, tells the household every day about the aunt's base and hypocritical tricks.

Stankes's Wife
Stankes's Wife is the unnamed wife of Stankes; she and Stankes dined with the narrator's household.

Mother-----
Mother----- is a house or public house opposite the Crown where the narrator, Mr. Davenport, Phillips, Jaspar Trice, and others sat, drank ale, and were merry until about nine at night.

The Crown
The Crown is an establishment or landmark opposite Mother----- near which the group gathered and drank ale.

The House
The house that the narrator's aunt agreed to quit as part of the settlement.

Mr. Barnwell
A man who supped with the narrator and later, as R. Barnwell, witnessed the delivery of the Sturtlow surrender.

J. Bowles
A man who came with Mr. Barnwell and supped with the narrator's group.

Old William Luffe
A man who paid up a bond of L20 and received the surrender of Sturtlow; Luffe acknowledged that the narrator's uncle had delivered the surrender to him.

The Narrator's Uncle
The narrator's uncle, who made a surrender of Sturtlow to the narrator and delivered it to Old William Luffe during his lifetime.<SEP>The Narrator's Uncle is the deceased relative whose will was read by The Narrator and Mr. Moore.

Surrender of Sturtlow
Legal document concerning the Sturtlow property, made by the narrator's uncle and later given to Old William Luffe.

Mr. Pigott
A man before whom Old William Luffe acknowledged the delivery of the surrender.

Bigglesworth
A place where the narrator stopped on his way to London to buy woollen stockings.

Hatfield
Town where the narrator arrived before noon and dined at Lord of Salisbury's Inn.<SEP>A place on the route to London where the diary narrator and the traveling companion bait their horses and walk through a great house.<SEP>A place where Mr. Whately is staying and from which Mrs. Whately expects to hear from her husband.

Lord of Salisbury's Inn
Inn in Hatfield where the narrator had a good dinner.

The Vineyard
A beautiful place near Hatfield that the narrator walked to alone after dinner.

Mr. Looker
The Lord of Salisbury's gardener who showed the narrator the house, chapel, and gardens.

Lord of Salisbury
Person whose gardener was Mr. Looker and whose property was shown to the narrator.

Mr. Eglin
Friend of Mr. Looker mentioned when describing Mr. Looker.

Smithfield
Place in London where the narrator set up his horse after arriving.

Uncle Fenner
An uncle of the narrator at whose house the narrator called in London.<SEP>A male relative of the narrator whose house the narrator and the narrator's wife visit.<SEP>A relative of the narrator at whose house the narrator and the narrator's wife call and find much company.<SEP>An uncle of the narrator; joins the narrator's father and the narrator in discussing a wife for Tom.<SEP>The narrator's uncle; present at an alehouse with the narrator's father while the narrator visited.<SEP>An uncle of the Narrator; his house is used as a meeting place by the Narrator and Narrator's Father.

The Narrator's Mother
The narrator's mother, at whose house the narrator called on the 22nd.

Batten
A person the narrator visited together with Sir W. Pen on the 23rd.<SEP>A man to whom the diarist made a visit.

Mrs. Michell
A woman the narrator talked with for a good while in Westminster Hall.<SEP>A woman with whom the diarist talked for a good while at Westminster Hall.

data.entity_name: The Hostess at Lord of Salisbury's Inn
data.content:
The Hostess at Lord of Salisbury's Inn
The woman who was the hostess at Lord of Salisbury's Inn and provided the narrator with a very good dinner.

William Luffe's Bond
A bond of L20 that Old William Luffe paid up on the afternoon before the narrator's journey.

Mrs. Palmer
The King's mistress, before whom the diarist sat at the theatre.

Uncle Thomas
The diarist's uncle, who met the diarist at the diarist's father's house to discuss an uncle's will.<SEP>The narrator's uncle who was to meet the following week for a reading of the Captain's will.<SEP>An uncle of the narrator; news reported that Uncle Thomas and his son went into the country without notice.

Aunt Wight
The wife of Uncle Wight; the diarist saw her when he called at their house.<SEP>A relative of the narrator whose house is the venue for a supper attended by the narrator, the narrator's wife, and Pall.<SEP>An aunt who receives a visit from Narrator's Mother and Aunt Bell.

Cozen Thomas Pepys
The diarist's cousin, with whom the diarist discusses the uncle's estate and will.

Sir G. Lane
A man who encounters the diarist and his cousin while they inspect a house for hire.

The Diarist's Father
The diarist's father, at whose house the diarist meets Uncle Thomas.<SEP>The father of the Diarist, who has gone to settle at Brampton and is furnished with borrowed money.

Brenoralt
A play the diarist saw for the first time; it seemed good but was ill acted.

Silver Tankard
A silver tankard belonging to the diarist and his wife that was stolen after a door was left open.

The Diarist's Father's House
The residence of the diarist's father, where the diarist went to meet Uncle Thomas and discuss the uncle's will.

The House For Hire
A property for hire that has a bill upon the door; it is described as a very pretty place and is walked around by Sir G. Lane, the diarist, and Cozen Thomas Pepys.

Diarist's Mother
Mother of the Diarist; visited by the Diarist, and believes a large fortune has fallen to her.

Aunt Bell
An aunt of the Diarist; present at the Diarist's mother's house and involved in the women's talk.<SEP>An aunt of the Narrator; comes to the Narrator's house for the first time to dine, then visits Aunt Wight.

Mrs. Ramsey
A woman present at the Diarist's mother's house, taking part in the conversation with the older women.

Mr. Hill of Cambridge
A man met at Pope's Head Alley; spoke about state affairs and told the Diarist that the King would be forced to favour Presbytery.

Pope's Head Alley
A place where the Diarist met Mr. Hill of Cambridge and women, and went into a tavern.

England
The country whose whole state, regarding the Church, Mr. Hill claimed had changed the previous day.<SEP>England is the country whose state as to the Church is mentioned at the outset.

The City
The city mentioned in Mr. Hill's political talk, which would leave the King if the King did not favour Presbytery.<SEP>The City denotes the political body of London that would abandon the King if Presbytery were not favoured.<SEP>The district of London to which Mr. Moore and The Narrator walk before parting.

Presbytery
Presbyterian form of church government; according to Mr. Hill, the King would be forced to favour it.<SEP>Presbytery is a system of church government; the King would be forced to favour Presbytery, otherwise the City would leave the King.

Parliament
The English Parliament; the Diarist, on inquiry, found that things there had changed.<SEP>Parliament is the English legislative body; Parliament is in disorder and its expected adjournment for two or three months was hindered for a day or two.<SEP>The legislative body that The King is expected to come and adjourn.<SEP>The legislative assembly in which public matters are described as being carried by young men.

The Church
The church whose state in England had changed on the previous day, according to Mr. Hill.<SEP>The church that the Narrator and his Wife attended on the Sunday, together with Mrs. Ramsay in the morning and again in the afternoon.

The Jovial Crew
A play seen by the Diarist at the Theatre; described as merry, innocent, and well performed.

Diarist's Journal
The written diary entries set down by the Diarist at night, covering the time since leaving London.

Papers of the Diarist's Uncle
Papers belonging to the Diarist's uncle that arrived by box from Brampton and gave the Diarist work.

Tavern at Pope's Head Alley
A tavern in Pope's Head Alley where Mr. Hill of Cambridge brought the Diarist and some women and gave them wine.

Will's Clock
A clock belonging to the Diarist's servant Will; Will lost it together with the Diarist's tankard.

Diarist's Tankard
A tankard belonging to the Diarist; Will lost it together with Will's clock.

Diarist's Deceased Uncle
The Diarist's late uncle whose papers were sent in a box from Brampton and whose inheritance is connected to the estate left to the Diarist.

King
The King is the monarch of England discussed in the account; the King would be forced to favour Presbytery to keep the City from leaving, and cannot do without the Lord Chancellor for policy and service.<SEP>Monarch mentioned in the passage. The King gives a handwritten warrant to the Chancellor, appears at Worcester House in a plain riding-suit and velvet cap, and receives money voted by the Parliament of Ireland.<SEP>Monarch mentioned alongside the Duke and Duchess; Mrs. Palmer is described as the King's mistress.

Church
Church is the religious institution whose state in England is the opening concern of the passage.<SEP>The church to which the narrator went after leaving the alehouse, where the narrator stayed through the sermon while the narrator's father's family appeared in mourning.

God
God is the deity from whom the Narrator hopes to receive forgiveness for breaking a vow to drink no wine.

Mr. Montagu
Mr. Montagu is the person in whose chamber at Westminster the Narrator heard a Frenchman play the guitar.

Frenchman
Frenchman is a friend of Monsieur Eschar who played the guitar extremely well in Mr. Montagu's chamber.

Monsieur Eschar
Monsieur Eschar is the person whose friend the Frenchman is.

Guitar
Guitar is the instrument played by the Frenchman in Mr. Montagu's chamber.

Mr. George Montagu
Mr. George Montagu is a man spoken to by the Narrator in the lobby of Westminster Hall; Mr. George Montagu discussed the ship for Lord Hinchingbroke and reported the political situation involving the Lord Chancellor.

Lord Hinchingbroke
Lord Hinchingbroke is a young lord who, with the other young gentlemen, resolved to go to France in a hired vessel from Rye rather than in a man of war.<SEP>A lord who became ill after the narrator gave him fruit and wine; was in great fear of smallpox.<SEP>A nobleman staying at My Lady's house who is recovering from illness and is found by the diarist to be gradually better.<SEP>A nobleman recovering from illness; sits up and walks about the chamber.<SEP>A lord from whom the narrator took leave at the Wardrobe; Lord Hinchingbroke rode with the brother toward Rye on the way to France.

Rye
Rye is the port from which Lord Hinchingbroke and the young gentlemen resolved to sail.<SEP>The town toward which Lord Hinchingbroke and the brother travelled by coach before reaching France.

Duke Of Buckingham
Duke Of Buckingham is a great man who, according to Mr. George Montagu, endeavours to undermine the Lord Chancellor.

Lord Of Bristoll
Lord Of Bristoll is a nobleman who, with the Duke of Buckingham, endeavours to undermine the Lord Chancellor.

Lord Of Sandwich
Lord Of Sandwich is the nobleman whose birthday was celebrated at the Wardrobe with many friends.

Captain Isham
Captain Isham is a person who was among the friends at the Wardrobe for Lord of Sandwich's birthday.<SEP>A captain who was part of the merry company with Mr. Townsend and shared the venison pasty.<SEP>An acquaintance of the narrator going with Mr Fanshaw toward Portugal.

Mr. Pargiter
Mr. Pargiter is a merchant who was also at the Wardrobe gathering.<SEP>A merchant who was also with the Narrator's company on the day of the dinner.

Mr. Townsend's Wife
Mr. Townsend's Wife is the unnamed wife of Mr. Townsend who was among the friends gathered at the Wardrobe for Lord Of Sandwich's birthday.

Captain Ferrers' Lady
The wife or companion of Captain Ferrers; included in the same merry dinner company as Mr. Townsend and others.<SEP>Captain Ferrers' Lady is the unnamed lady associated with Captain Ferrers and was among the friends gathered at the Wardrobe.

Lord Of Sandwich's Birthday
Lord Of Sandwich's Birthday is the occasion being celebrated at the Wardrobe, attended by the Narrator, his wife, and many friends.

data.entity_name: The Narrator's Vow To Drink No Wine
data.content:
The Narrator's Vow To Drink No Wine
A vow made by The Narrator at the beginning of the week to drink no wine for that week; The Narrator broke the vow on the day described and hoped God would forgive the breaking of it.

Townsend's Wife
The wife of Mr. Townsend; part of the merry dinner party that ate venison pasty.

Captain Cooke
A captain who called on Mr. Townsend after dinner, joined the Narrator and Mr. Townsend at a tavern, and sang in what the Narrator considered the best manner in the world.

Lady Jem
A young woman who, with Pall, was taken by water through the bridge by the Narrator and his wife to see ships and the Narrator's house.

Lady Jem and Pall's Mother
The mother of Lady Jem and Pall, referred to as "my Lady"; had recently gone alone with the Narrator's Wife to look at the Narrator's house while the Narrator was away.

Mrs. Ramsay
A visitor who came to see the Narrator and his Wife on a Sunday, went to church, and dined with them.

Sir W. Pen's Daughter
The daughter of Sir W. Pen, recently arrived from Ireland; described by the Narrator's Wife as a very plain girl, not a great beauty.

Sir R. Ford
A knight who owns a house that Sir R. Slingsby and the Narrator inspected; he may be persuaded to part with it for the office.<SEP>A man who agrees to have his house added to the office to enlarge its quarters.<SEP>Person whose house is being considered for addition to the Office.

Narrator's Brother Tom
The Narrator's brother, who dined with the Narrator after work at the office.

Sir R. Ford's House
The house owned by Sir R. Ford, inspected by the Narrator and Sir R. Slingsby because it could conveniently be added to the office.<SEP>House owned by Sir R. Ford, considered for addition to the Office, rent L200 per annum.

The Tavern
A tavern near the dinner venue where the Narrator, Mr. Townsend, and Captain Cooke went after dinner and where Captain Cooke sang.

Ireland
The country from which Sir W. Pen's daughter had recently come.<SEP>Place from which Mrs. Margarett Pen had recently come before Samuel Pepys saw her.<SEP>The country from which Colonel Dillon returned before courting the Butler sisters.

Narrator's Linen
The linen belonging to the Narrator, given to him by his wife; he put it up and intended to keep it in his own custody.

Mother
The mother of The Narrator, who is sent for by ill Aunt Fenner and spends freely based on property left by the uncle.<SEP>The narrator's mother, who is found with the narrator's father in a discontent at the father's house.

Uncle
The uncle of The Narrator, whose bequest to the family enables the Mother's spending.

Aunt Fenner
The aunt of The Narrator, who is extremely ill and sends for the Mother.<SEP>The narrator's aunt, who was near death.<SEP>Relative of Pepys whose death is recorded in the passage before the diary entry dated 20th.<SEP>A female relative of the narrator who dies on the day recorded.

Charles Glassecocke
The cousin of The Narrator, who, though ill, travels to the country to see his brother John Glassecocke.

John Glassecocke
The brother of Charles Glassecocke, who is dying in the country.

Singing Master
The singing teacher of The Narrator, who gives The Narrator a lesson in the morning.

Lady
The woman with whom The Narrator dines at the Wardrobe.

Dr. Thomas Pepys
A man met at the Wardrobe, said to be a silly talking fellow but very good-natured.

Mr. Salisbury
A limner met in Fleet Street who has become a great limner in less than two years.<SEP>Limner, or painter, whom Samuel Pepys met in Fleet Street; he had become excellent in less than two years and earned a great deal of money.

House of Lords
The upper house of Parliament that challenges the privilege of not having its houses searched and refuses to pass the House of Commons bill.

House of Commons
The lower house of Parliament whose bill for searching for pamphlets and seditious books is denied by the House of Lords.

White Hall
A place The Narrator visits after his singing lesson.<SEP>A location where the narrator attended a meeting in a chamber over the gate.<SEP>The location where the narrator met Lord Privy Seal in his chamber over the gate.<SEP>Royal building in London where the narrator heard news about Lord General Monk.

Fleet Street
A street in London where The Narrator inquires about the Assizes and encounters Mr. Salisbury.<SEP>Street where Samuel Pepys met Mr. Salisbury.

Tangier
The place or business that is the subject of the office meeting attended by The Narrator.

data.entity_name: Bill for Searching for Pamphlets and Seditious Books
data.content:
Bill for Searching for Pamphlets and Seditious Books
A bill proposed by the House of Commons for searching out pamphlets and seditious books, refused passage by the House of Lords.

Assizes
Court sessions that begin at Cambridge and Huntingdon, the schedule of which The Narrator seeks in Fleet Street.<SEP>Court sessions held at Castle Hill, attended by judges and visited by the narrator.

Father's House in London
A house in London owned by Father; Father considers whether to profit from it or leave it to Tom.

The Trade
The occupation that Tom might set up in another place; Tom declines to set up The Trade unless Father leaves the London house to Tom.

Mr. Whore
Ingenious friend of Mr. Salisbury who joined Samuel Pepys and Mr. Salisbury at Hercules Pillars.

Mrs. Margarett Pen
Woman who had recently come from Ireland and traveled with Samuel Pepys and others by coach to Walthamstow.

Mrs. Browne
Host in Walthamstow whom Samuel Pepys and his party visited a-gossiping; she received six silver spoons for her boy.

Dr. Thos. Pepys
Man who dined with Samuel Pepys at noon.

Tom Pepys
Samuel Pepys's brother, who came to Samuel after dinner before Samuel set out for Cambridge.

Hercules Pillars
Drinking house where Samuel Pepys, Mr. Salisbury, and Mr. Whore sat together.

Walthamstow
Place to which Samuel Pepys and his companions traveled by coach to visit Mrs. Browne.

Ware
Town where Samuel Pepys rode and stayed overnight on his way toward Cambridge.<SEP>A town where the narrator stays overnight after riding out on the first night of the journey.

The Tamer Tamed
A play performed at The Theatre; Samuel Pepys judged it well done.

Singing-Master
Samuel Pepys's music teacher, who came to Samuel Pepys on the morning of the 31st.

Samuel Pepys's Wife
Wife of Samuel Pepys; traveled by coach with Samuel Pepys, the two Sir Williams, and Mrs. Margarett Pen to Walthamstow.<SEP>Wife of Samuel Pepys; mentioned as being looked askew upon and as dining with Samuel Pepys.

Quaker Fellmonger
A Quaker and dealer in hides who discourses with the narrator on the way to Ware and confesses his wicked life until two years before.<SEP>A Quaker and dealer in hides who conversed with Samuel Pepys while riding toward Ware and spoke about his past wickedness.

Nurse's Husband
Husband of a nurse; made unflattering remarks about Lady Batten's reputation relating to a man who left her an estate.

Barkway
A place where the narrator stops to drink and meets the letter-carrier of Cambridge.

Letter-Carrier of Cambridge
A mail carrier from Cambridge who rides with the narrator from Barkway all the way to Cambridge because the narrator's horse is tired and the narrator is wet with rain.

Castle Hill
A location in Cambridge where the judges were holding the Assizes.

The Doctor
A brother of Roger Pepys who dines with the narrator and Claxton at Trinity Hall.

Claxton
A person who dines with the narrator and the Doctor at Trinity Hall.

Trinity Hall
A Cambridge college where the narrator dines with the Doctor and Claxton.

The Rose
A tavern or inn in Cambridge where the narrator sits drinking with Mr. Pechell, Sanchy, and others.

Mr. Pechell
One of the companions with whom the narrator drinks at the Rose.

Sanchy
One of the companions with whom the narrator drinks at the Rose.

Dr. Gunning
An old doctor in the University who is singled out as being held in high regard over better scholars.

University
The academic institution in Cambridge where old doctors hold high positions over better scholars.

Uncle Talbot
An uncle of the narrator who attends church with the narrator and Roger Pepys at Impington.

Uncle Talbot's Will
The will of the narrator's uncle, the main business for which the narrator consults Roger Pepys.

Parson
The clergyman at the Impington church who preaches a good plain sermon and addresses the narrator and Roger Pepys as "Right worshipfull and dearly beloved."

Judges
The group of judges present at the Assizes at Castle Hill in Cambridge when the narrator arrived.

Old Doctors
Senior academic doctors in the University who, according to the narrator's companions, are raised high above better scholars at the University.

Public Matters
Public or political affairs that the narrator and others discussed after supper at Impington.

Young Men in Parliament
Young parliamentary members described as profane swearing fellows who labor to oppose everything moved by serious men.

Serious Men in Parliament
Parliamentary members whose serious motions were opposed by the young men.

Cousin Nightingale
A female relative of The Narrator living at Yelling; the cousin advises The Narrator about obtaining a surrender of Graveley lands.

Chancler
A man whom The Narrator met at an alehouse in Graveley.

Jackson
One of The Narrator's tenants for Cotton Closes; Jackson meets The Narrator at an alehouse in Graveley.

Thomas Trice
A man also called Thos. Trice and Tom Trice; The Narrator drinks with Thomas Trice at Huntingdon, and Thomas Trice later goes to Brampton and to Goody Gorum's.

Stanton
A place where The Narrator must stay for a while because of rain and where The Narrator borrows a coat from a man.

Yelling
The village where Cousin Nightingale has a pretty house and where The Narrator visits Cousin Nightingale.

Graveley
A village that The Narrator goes to after Yelling; The Narrator stops at an alehouse there and meets Chancler and Jackson.

Graveley Lands
Land for which The Narrator wishes to obtain a surrender, with advice from Cousin Nightingale.

Cotton Closes
Land held by Jackson as a tenant of The Narrator.

The Judges
The judges whom The Narrator expected to be in Huntingdon but who had not yet arrived there when The Narrator passed through.

Gorum's House
The house or establishment of Goody Gorum, visited by the diary narrator and the father, where Tom Trice is present.

Baldwick
A town on the diary narrator's route to London where the narrator stops for the night, has supper, and visits a handsome church.

Baldwick Landlady
The landlady of the Baldwick lodging where the diary narrator stays; described as a pretty woman whose husband is present.

Baldwick Landlady's Husband
The husband of the Baldwick landlady, present at the lodging when the diary narrator stays there.

Church at Baldwick
A handsome church in Baldwick that the diary narrator goes to see before supper.

Quakers
A religious group that the diary narrator observes continuing and rather growing than lessening in Baldwick and other places.<SEP>Religious group described as continuing and growing rather than lessening.

Venison Traveller
A man riding toward London with venison in panniers; had ridden part of the previous night's road with the diary narrator and later traveled with the narrator after sharing breakfast.

Great House at Hatfield
A large house in Hatfield through all of whose courts the diary narrator walks.

Pretty Dog at Hatfield
A pretty dog at Hatfield that follows the diary narrator and that the narrator would like to steal but cannot.

Lord Roberts
The Lord Privy Seal whom the diary narrator is to wait upon during the narrator's month; Lord Roberts fails to appear at Whitehall and at the Privy Seal.

Privy Seal
The office or institution of the Lord Privy Seal where a Seal day is to be held and where the diary narrator is required to attend in the narrator's month.<SEP>The government office where Mons. Eschar waited for the warrant.<SEP>A place or office the Narrator goes to in the morning.<SEP>Office at which a seal was held in the morning and which the narrator attended.<SEP>Government office to which the narrator was summoned; the narrator found an item belonging to the Lord Chancellor there.

Seal Day
An official day of sealing at the Privy Seal, scheduled for the day after the diary narrator learns about it.

Diary Narrator's House
The narrator's home in London, where the narrator returns after reaching London and where Dean Fuller comes to see the narrator.

Father's House
The residence of the narrator's father where the narrator went for supper.<SEP>The residence of the diary narrator's father; after arriving in London, the narrator finds all well there.

My Lady's House
The house of My Lady, where the diary narrator goes with Dean Fuller and meets Mr. Moore.

Lord Privy Seal
The office-holder who met the narrator in his chamber at White Hall and asked what deputation the narrator had from My Lord.<SEP>Official who did not have the seal at Worcester House; later went to a house in Chelsy where Pepys and Mr. Moore examined and sealed a document with the official.

Mons. Eschar
A man who waited at the Privy Seal for the warrant for Lord Sandwich and then accompanied the narrator to visit La Belle Pierce.<SEP>A man who drank with the narrator at the tavern near the Savoy and argued against English music in favor of French music, angering Mr. Mage.

Dr. Pierce's Brother
A soldier and brother of Dr. Pierce who drank with the narrator and others at the tavern near the Savoy.

Mr. Pierces
A person whose son-in-law brought the narrator news about a dying man.

Son-In-Law Of Mr. Pierces
A son-in-law of Mr. Pierces who came to the office with word that his father was dying and desired the narrator's visit.

The Dying Man
The father of Mr. Pierces's son-in-law, who was reported to be dying, asked the narrator to come before death, and received the narrator's promise to help his wife and family.

Mr. Hater
A man who brought news that his wife was in labour and came to fetch the narrator's wife.

Mr. Hater's Wife
The wife of Mr. Hater who was falling into labour during the day.

Clerks Of The Privy Seal
The clerks employed at the Privy Seal, who were reportedly treated severely and ill by My Lord.

The Privy Seal
The office to which the narrator went on business and where My Lord was expected but did not appear.<SEP>A government office the diarist visits before going to Whitehall.<SEP>An office the narrator attends to have documents sealed.

The Tavern Near The Savoy
The tavern next to the Savoy where the narrator drank with Mons. Eschar, Mr. Moore, Dr. Pierce's brother, and met Mr. Mage.

The Secretarys
The two office-holders referred to collectively as both of the Secretarys, who swore The Narrator as My Lord's deputy.

Dr. Pierce
The physician whose brother, a soldier, was taken by The Narrator to the tavern near the Savoy.

The Savoy
The building or place next to which the tavern stood where The Narrator drank with Mons. Eschar, Mr. Moore, and Dr. Pierce's brother.

Lord Sandwich
A nobleman referred to as "My Lord" and "my Lord of Sandwich"; the narrator is sworn as Lord Sandwich's deputy, and Lord Sandwich's preparations for Portugal require a 5,000-pound warrant.<SEP>A lord confirmed to be sick ashore at Alicante; the narrator fears for his family if he should die.<SEP>The man referred to in the text as "my Lord"; the vessel sent by the narrator carried Lord Sandwich's things toward Lynn.<SEP>A lord recovering from fever; Lord Sandwich lay sick at Alicante, was twice bled, sent a letter to the narrator, and had money arranged for a departure to Portugal.<SEP>A lord who is in the Straits and has recently recovered from a serious sickness at Alicante.

The Secretaries
The two officials who administered the narrator's oath as Lord Sandwich's deputy.

La Belle Pierce
A lady visited by the narrator and Mons. Eschar; La Belle Pierce was very pregnant and in the company of Mrs. Clifford.<SEP>A woman visited by the narrator after the narrator heard about Lord General Monk.

Mrs. Clifford
A pretty lady who was with La Belle Pierce during the visit.

Mrs. Hater
A woman in labor whom the narrator heard had not yet delivered and was still in pain.

The Chambermaid
A recently hired maid described as very ugly but seemingly good; The Chambermaid was to begin work in about three weeks.

Coffee House
The meeting place where the narrator and his father found Uncle Wight.

Clerkenwell
A place the narrator went to on the afternoon of the 11th.

The Merry Devil of Edmonton
A merry play shown at the Theatre; the narrator saw it for the first time and was pleased.

Captain's Will
The will of a Captain, to be read the following week before Uncle Wight and Uncle Thomas for their satisfaction.

The Warrant for L5,000
A warrant for 5,000 pounds for Lord Sandwich's preparations for Portugal, awaited by Mons. Eschar at the Privy Seal.

The Official at White Hall
An unnamed official who received the narrator in a chamber over the gate at White Hall, asked what deputation the narrator had from Lord Sandwich, was satisfied by the narrator's sworn status as deputy, and then caused Mr. Moore to read over the bills.

The Two Young Gentlemen
Two unnamed young gentlemen at My Lady's who were taken by the narrator, together with the two ladies and Captain Ferrers, to the Theatre and afterward to the narrator's house.

The Two Ladies
Two unnamed ladies at My Lady's who were taken by the narrator, together with the two young gentlemen and Captain Ferrers, to the Theatre and afterward to the narrator's house.

The Narrator's House
The narrator's home, where his father visited him and where the narrator brought the theatre party by coach and gave them fruit and wine.

Our Own Church
The church the narrator attended in the forenoon on the 11th before going to Clerkenwell in the afternoon.

Frances Butler's Sister
The unnamed sister of Frances Butler; the second of the two fair Butlers seen at church.

Colonel Dillon
A colonel who has returned from Ireland and courts the Butler sisters, attending church with them.

Ned Pickering
An acquaintance met at Graye's Inn walks who told the narrator about the King's stag hunt.<SEP>A man the narrator met; he walked in St. James's Park with the narrator, complained of the Court, and dined at the Wardrobe.

Sir H. Wright
The person at whose house Lord Crew is currently staying.<SEP>The host with whom Lord Crew is staying.

Anthony Brewer
The playwright (also called Tony Brewer) whom the initials T.B. in the Stationers' entry may name as author of the 1608 comedy.

William Shakespeare
One of the authors to whom the 1608 comedy was attributed without authority.

Michael Drayton
One of the authors to whom the 1608 comedy was attributed without authority.

Clerkenwell Church
A church attended by the narrator in the afternoon specifically to see the fair Butlers.

Alicante
The place where Lord Sandwich lies ill ashore.<SEP>The place where Lord Sandwich lay sick and had not yet left when the letter was written.<SEP>A city where Lord Sandwich was sick and from which he has recently recovered.

Sir H. Wright's House
The house where Lord Crew is staying while his own new house is being prepared.

Lord Crew's New House
The new house being made fit for Lord Crew, where he is not yet residing.

The Stag Hunt
A great hunt of a stag held the previous day with the King, who wore out the other riders' horses.

The 1608 Comedy
An anonymous comedy acted at the Globe and first printed in 1608; its Stationers' entry credits T.B., possibly Anthony Brewer, and it has also been ascribed to Shakespeare and Drayton without authority.

Smallpox
The disease that those caring for Lord Hinchingbroke feared he had contracted.<SEP>A disease feared by My Lady; the reason for sending the sons away.

T. B.
The initials given as the author of the 1608 comedy in the original Stationers' entry; the text notes that they may stand for Tony or Anthony Brewer.

Narrator's Own Church
The church referred to as "our own church," which the narrator attended in the forenoon on the 11th (Lord's day).

Narrator's Office
The office where the narrator spent the morning of the 12th before going home in the afternoon.

Lord Sandwich's Family
The unnamed family of Lord Sandwich whose possible misfortune the narrator fears if Lord Sandwich should die.

My Young Lord
A young lord found very ill at The Wardrobe; the illness causes concern and prompts others to be sent away.

Sidney
Son of My Lady; one of the three sons sent to Narrator's House.

Oliver
Son of My Lady; one of the three sons sent to Narrator's House.

John
Son of My Lady; one of the three sons sent to Narrator's House.<SEP>The Narrator's brother, found in bed at eight o'clock, which vexed the Narrator.

My Mother
Mother of the Narrator; described as a very simple woman and involved in near-high words with the Narrator.

Mrs. Cordery
A woman who comes to take leave of My Father.<SEP>A woman visited by the narrator's wife and Lady Sandwich's children; the visit took place before the narrator's father went into the country.

My Uncle Thomas
An uncle of the Narrator; has two sons, keeps The Caveat, and later promises to withdraw it.

My Uncle Wight
An uncle of the Narrator; comes to Mr. Rawlinson's by appointment.

The Caveat
A legal objection raised by My Uncle Thomas, which My Uncle Thomas promises to withdraw.

Lord of Sandwich
A lord whose health troubles the Narrator.

The Navy
The naval force described as being in a condition of lack of money.<SEP>The naval force whose lack of money is reported to the Duke of York and whose bills are sold at a loss on the Exchange.

Old Papers of Difference
Old papers held at My Father's house concerning a past disagreement between the Narrator and My Wife; the Narrator took them away from My Father's house.

The Duchess
The royal duchess who dines with Sir H. Finch and attends the Opera with the King and Duke.

Sir H. Finch
A reader at the Temple who hosts the King, Duke, and Duchess for a dinner in great state.

The Dolphin
A tavern where Sir W. Pen and the diarist meet Sir W. Batten.<SEP>A place, apparently a tavern or inn, where Sir W. Batten was and where the narrator and Sir W. Pen went.

Paul's
A place near the Wardrobe where Sir W. Pen sets down Captain Ferrers and later carries the diarist.<SEP>A place in London reached by the narrator while walking; the narrator parts from a walking companion there.

The Witts
A play performed at the Opera for the first time with scenes and praised by the diarist.<SEP>A play performed at the Opera; the narrator saw it and liked it exceedingly.<SEP>A play shown at the Opera; the narrator shows it to the narrator's wife and is highly pleased with it, although the narrator has seen it twice before.

The Council
The governing body to which the Duke of York planned to speak about the Navy's lack of money.

Mr. Falconer of Woolwich
A person from Woolwich who was made drunk by the narrator and companions at the Dolphin.

Tom Whitton
A Controller's clerk whose burial was attended by the office clerks.

The Controller
Unnamed official for whom Tom Whitton served as a clerk.

Tom Fuller
A famous man who died of the fever.

Dr. Nichols
Dean of Paul's who died of the fever.

St. Paul's Cathedral
The cathedral for which Dr. Nichols was Dean, referred to in the passage as Paul's.

Lord General Monk
A prominent general who was very dangerously ill during the sickly time.<SEP>A general reported to be continuing very ill.

Fever
A sort of fever causing a sickly time in the City and country.

Father of the Narrator
The father of the narrator, who dined with the narrator and later went out with the narrator on business.

Dr. John Williams
A man met in an alehouse in Shoe Lane, well acquainted with matters of Gravely, whom the narrator expected to be useful.

Shoe Lane
Street where Dr. John Williams was met in an alehouse.

St. James's Park
Park where the narrator and Ned Pickering walked and found notable alterations.<SEP>A park where the narrator walked and saw many fowl.

The Court
The royal court, criticized by Ned Pickering for lewdness and beggary.<SEP>The court to which one of its judges belongs; that judge swears the narrator and the narrator's father.<SEP>The royal court, described as being in very ill condition.<SEP>Royal court associated with lewdness and beggary in the diary text.

Queen of Bohemia
A royal woman who was at the Opera, brought there by Lord Craven.

Lord Craven
A man who brought the Queen of Bohemia to the Opera.<SEP>A nobleman mentioned at the start of the passage as having brought something or someone.

Devil Tavern
A tavern where Captain Ferrers, the narrator, and another person drank.<SEP>A tavern at which the narrator, the captain, and another person drank.<SEP>A tavern where the narrator and Mr. Bostock drink.

Narrator's Children
The narrator's children, who dined at home with the narrator.

Burial of Tom Whitton
The burial ceremony for Tom Whitton attended by the office clerks.

The Captain
A captain accompanied by the narrator and another person to the Devil tavern.

Dr. Tom Pepys
A Pepys family member and doctor; dines with the narrator and the narrator's father.

Mr. Sidney
A companion taken by the narrator and the narrator's wife to Lady Sandwich's house to see Lord Hinchingbroke.

Lady Sandwich
Mother of the children sent for to dinner; hostess at the house where Lord Hinchingbroke is visited.<SEP>A lady who gave birth to a daughter on the previous day and is reported to be well.<SEP>Woman referred to as "my Lady"; Lady Sandwich's bedside was visited by the narrator, and Lady Sandwich talked with the narrator about Edward Montagu's disposal of L5000.

Clarendon
The Lord Chancellor, also referred to as my Lord Chancellor and the Chancellor; procured grants from the king and was connected to a royal warrant for Sir Stephen Fox.

Sir Stephen Fox
Person instructed by the King's warrant to pay L20,000 to the Chancellor.<SEP>Person named in the king's warrant; directed to pay the Chancellor the sum of £20,000.

Lynn
Town to which the narrator sent a vessel with the Lord's things.

Soale Bay
Bay where the narrator's sent vessel was reported to have put in.

Vessel
Ship sent by the narrator to Lynn with the Lord's things and later reported in Soale Bay.

Lady Sandwich's Children
Children of Lady Sandwich who were sent for to dinner and who accompanied the narrator's wife by coach to the narrator's father's house and then to Mrs. Cordery's.

Little Billet
A small letter or note given by the king to Clarendon; it contained a warrant written in the king's own hand.

Warrant
A royal document written in the king's own hand-writing and contained in the little billet; it directed Sir Stephen Fox to pay the Chancellor, Clarendon, the sum of L20,000.

Chancellor
Royal official who receives L20,000 under the King's warrant, receives L5,000 out of money voted by the Parliament of Ireland, receives another L20,000 to clear a mortgage on Clarendon Park, and is impeached by the Commons.

King's Warrant
Handwritten royal document delivered to the Chancellor; the document directs Sir Stephen Fox to pay L20,000 to the Chancellor.

Parliament of Ireland
Legislative body that voted money to the King; the Chancellor received L5,000 from that money.

Commons
Legislative body that brought impeachment against the Chancellor; the Chancellor answered with a vindication.

Chancellor's Vindication
Written defense produced by the Chancellor against the Commons' impeachment; the vindication mentions L5,000 received from money voted by the Parliament of Ireland.

Clarendon Park
Property on which a mortgage was cleared using L20,000 given to the Chancellor.

Dunkirk
Location involved in a sale that brought money from France; sale proceeds were believed to have paid the Chancellor L20,000.

Chelsy
Place to which Pepys and Mr. Moore traveled by coach to meet the Lord Privy Seal.

Mr. Marsh
Lutenist encountered near the Neate houses together with Mr. Marsh's wife; the couple walked with Pepys to Westminster.

Mr. Marsh's Wife
Wife of the lutenist Mr. Marsh; present with Mr. Marsh near the Neate houses and walked with Mr. Marsh and Pepys to Westminster.

Father Fenner
The father of Will Joyce, from whom Will Joyce expects mourning money for himself and his brother.

Mrs. Terry
A daughter of Mr. Whately who proposes her sister as a wife for Brother Tom.

Mr. Whately
A father of Mrs. Terry and of the young woman proposed for Brother Tom; is staying at Hatfield.

Mrs. Whately
Mother of the young woman proposed for Brother Tom; discusses the match and offers £200 down with the daughter.

Mrs. Whately's Daughter
A young woman proposed as a wife for Brother Tom; daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Whately and sister of Mrs. Terry.

Brother Tom
The narrator's brother, for whom a wife is sought from the Whately family.

Will Joyce
An acquaintance of the narrator who is angry about the amount of mourning money from Father Fenner.

The Young Lady
Lady Sandwich's newborn daughter, reported to be well.

The Sessions
A court or judicial session referred to as "the Sessions," at which a great deal of company was gathered on the 22nd, in addition to the company at Uncle Fenner's house.

Wife
The narrator's wife, who accompanies the narrator to Uncle Fenner's house, Aunt Wight's house, the Opera, and the Wardrobe.

W. Joyce
The person at whose house the narrator's wife is waiting by appointment before the narrator takes her to the Opera.

Captain Holmes
The captain who brought the great baboon with him from Guiny to Sir W. Batten's house.

Great Baboon
A large baboon brought from Guiny by Captain Holmes, resembling a man in most things and displayed at Sir W. Batten's house.

Guiny
The place from which Captain Holmes brought the great baboon.

Judge of the Court
One of the judges of the Court before whom the narrator and the narrator's father are sworn after being brought there by Tom Trice.

Cook's Shop
A cook's shop where Dr. Williams and the narrator went together and ate a bit of mutton.

The Creature
A manlike creature referred to as “it”; the Narrator believes it is a monster born of a man and a she-baboon and that it already understands much English.

Sir Rd. Ford
The owner of a house that the Narrator and the Comptroller view and agree to rent for L200 per annum.

Capt. Isham
A captain who is about to voyage to Portugal and who calls on the Narrator to take his leave and to collect letters for My Lord.

Betterton
An actor who performs the part of Prince Hamlet in “Hamlet, Prince of Denmark” and whose performance is praised by the Narrator.

Downes
A source who records that Betterton was taught by Sir William Davenant and that the character of Hamlet was one of Betterton’s masterpieces.

Taylor of the Blackfriars
An actor from the Blackfriars theatre who had acted the part of Hamlet and who was instructed by Shakespeare himself.

Shakespeare
The playwright who instructed Taylor of the Blackfriars in acting the part of Hamlet.<SEP>Playwright mentioned as having instructed someone in the diary text.

Mr. Spong
An acquaintance whom the Narrator meets while going home and takes to the Sampson in Paul’s Churchyard.

Lady Batten's Daughter
The daughter of My Lady Batten; she joins her mother in looking askew at the Narrator’s wife.

The Sampson in Paul's Churchyard
A place in Paul’s Churchyard, likely a tavern, where the Narrator and Mr. Spong stay until late.

Hamlet, Prince of Denmark
A play seen by the Narrator at the Opera; it is performed with scenery and features Betterton in the title role.

Prince Hamlet
The title character of “Hamlet, Prince of Denmark”; the part performed by Betterton.

Restitution
The subject of Mr. Mills’s sermon, which discourses on the necessity of making restitution.

Theatrical Scenery
Scenery or stage scenes used in theatrical productions; the play Hamlet, Prince of Denmark was done with scenes very well, and Sir William Davenport introduced the use of such scenery.

Sir Rd. Ford's House
A house owned by Sir Rd. Ford, viewed again by the Narrator and the Comptroller; the group agreed to give Sir Rd. Ford L200 per annum for it.

Narrator's Mother
Mother of the narrator; expected to go into the country with Pall and the narrator's father.<SEP>The mother of the narrator; attended dinner at the house of Thos Pepys the Executor.<SEP>The mother of the Narrator; dines at the Narrator's house and later visits Aunt Wight with Aunt Bell.<SEP>The mother of the Narrator, who is expected to come to Brampton after her husband settles things there.

Maid Jane
The narrator's maid for three years; she leaves service to go to her mother in the country.

Lady at the Wardrobe
A lady at the Wardrobe whom the narrator visits.

Antipodes
A play seen at the Theatre; described as containing much mirth but no great matter else.

Mr. Bostock
A former clerk of Mr. Phelps; met at the Theatre by the narrator and later drinking at the Devil Tavern with the narrator.

Mr. Phelps
A man for whom Mr. Bostock formerly worked as a clerk.

Broker's Daughter
A woman whose father is a broker; proposed as a wife for Tom.<SEP>A young woman with a large portion; the proposed bride for Tom.

Ned
A servant of the narrator's father; the father dismissed the servant, angering Ned's friends.

Thomas, Son of Uncle Thomas
The son of Uncle Thomas; the son went into the country with Uncle Thomas without giving notice.

Letter from Lord Sandwich
A letter dated 22 July that the narrator found at home; the letter reported Lord Sandwich's recovery.

Mr. Fanshaw
An acquaintance of the narrator about to travel to Portugal; met by the narrator at the Crane Tavern.

Crane Tavern at the Stocks
The tavern where the narrator met by appointment and took leave of Mr Fanshaw and Captain Isham.

Lord Hinchingbroke's Brother
The brother who accompanied Lord Hinchingbroke by coach toward Rye and France.

L5000
The sum of money whose disposal by Mr Edward Montagu was discussed in connection with Lord Sandwich's departure for Portugal.

Thos. Pepys (Executor)
Cousin of the narrator described as the Executor; Thos. Pepys hosted a dinner attended by the narrator, the narrator's wife, father, and mother.

Mother, Friend of Ned
A mother who was a friend of Ned and was encountered in the street together with the son; she was angry at the narrator's father for dismissing Ned.

Son, Friend of Ned
A son who was a friend of Ned and was encountered in the street together with the mother; he was angry at the narrator's father for dismissing Ned.

The Jov
A play whose quoted title is truncated in the input as "The Jov"; the narrator and the narrator's wife watched it at the Theatre.

Balty
The brother of Narrator's Wife; is in a difficult condition that prompts Narrator's Wife to ask for assistance.

Aunt Pepys
A relative connected to a £200 bond that is the subject of legal consultation.

Mr. Evans
A tailor; father of a daughter considered as a potential wife for Tom; meets the Narrator and Narrator's Father at an alehouse.

Duke
A royal duke present at the Theatre during "The Joviall Crew".<SEP>Nobleman mentioned alongside the King and the Duchess.

Duchess
A duchess present at the Theatre during "The Joviall Crew".<SEP>Noblewoman mentioned alongside the King and the Duke.

Madame Palmer
A woman present at the Theatre during "The Joviall Crew".<SEP>Woman referred to as Madame Palmer and Mrs. Palmer; described as the King's mistress, and Samuel Pepys sat before her.

Mr. Evans's Daughter
The daughter of Mr. Evans; considered as a wife for Tom.

The Joviall Crew
A mirthful play performed at The Theatre and watched by the Narrator and Narrator's Wife.

Aunt Pepys's £200 Bond
A bond worth £200 involving Aunt Pepys, about which legal advice on interest is sought.

Counterfeit Letter
A false letter written by the Narrator to Sir W. Pen pretending to come from the thief who stole Sir W. Pen's tankard.

Dr. Williams' Attorney Friend
An unnamed attorney who is a friend of Dr. Williams; the Narrator and Dr. Williams go to look for this attorney to advise about Aunt Pepys's £200 bond.

Mr Evans
A tailor who is asked about giving his daughter to Tom for marriage, but who refuses because his estate is too great to give where no present possession exists except a trade and house.

Mr Evans's Daughter
The daughter of Mr Evans, considered as a prospective wife for Tom.

Narrator's Lady
The woman referred to as 'my Lady' by the Narrator, bedridden at the Wardrobe, whom he visits after dinner.

Lady Jemimah
A lady encountered by the Narrator at Bartholomew Fair while watching dancing monkeys, later going with him into Christ's Hospital.

Lady Paulina
A lady encountered by the Narrator at Bartholomew Fair while watching dancing monkeys, later going with him into Christ's Hospital.

Mr Pickering
A man who is with Lady Jemimah and Lady Paulina at Bartholomew Fair and later enters Christ's Hospital with them.

Madamoiselle
A young lady among the party who watches the monkeys dance and later receives fairings and baubles.<SEP>A woman accompanying Lady Jemimah, Lady Paulina, and Mr Pickering at Bartholomew Fair, later entering Christ's Hospital.

Luellin
An acquaintance who comes to the Narrator at the office, goes with him to a tavern and Bartholomew Fair, and later parts from him near Ludgate.

Son of Lord Somersett
A son of Lord Somersett, a man known to the Narrator's Wife from France, encountered at Drury Lane, whom the Narrator avoids.

Drury Lane
The street or theatre district in London where the Narrator and his wife see a French comedy.

Holborn
The place in London where the Narrator and his father take leave of each other.

Ludgate
The place in London toward which the Narrator and Luellin walk before parting.

Bartholomew Fair
The fair attended by the Narrator, Luellin, and later Lady Jemimah, Lady Paulina, Mr Pickering, and Madamoiselle.

Christ's Hospital
The charitable institution the Narrator enters after the fair with Lady Jemimah, Lady Paulina, Mr Pickering, and Madamoiselle.

Lord Somersett
A nobleman mentioned as the father of the son whom Narrator's Wife knew in France and met at Drury Lane; Lord Somersett is not present in the scene.

French Comedy
A theatrical comedy performed at Drury Lane, described as ill done, nasty, out of order, and poor, with only the farce giving any pleasure.

Dancing Monkeys
A group of monkeys at Bartholomew Fair performing dances, watched by The Narrator and by Lady Jemimah, Lady Paulina, Mr Pickering, and Madamoiselle.

The Ladies
A group of women whom the Diarist accompanies to Christ's Hospitall and for whom Mr. Pickering buys fairings and the Diarist gives baubles.

Mr. Pickering
A man in the party who buys fairings for the ladies at Christ's Hospitall.

Christ's Hospitall
A charitable institution in London that the party visits and where fairings are bought.

Mrs. Crispe
A lady who told My Lady that she intends to get the King to be godfather to her newborn daughter.

Mrs. Crispe's Daughter
The newborn baby girl for whom Mrs. Crispe hopes the King will be godfather.

Fenchurch Street
A London street to which Mr. Moore escorts the Diarist and where the Mitre is located.

Jane
The Diarist's maid who has recently gone away.

The Diarist's Mother
The mother of the Diarist, with whom Pall is to go into the country.

The Straits
The sea area where Lord Sandwich is located.

Monkeys
A troop of performing monkeys that danced when they could be brought to do so, though the Diarist found sitting in their company unpleasant.

data.entity_name: The Lady Staying at Mrs. Crispe's House
data.content:
The Lady Staying at Mrs. Crispe's House
An unnamed woman lodging at Mrs. Crispe's house whom Mrs. Crispe intended to use as a means to persuade the King to be godfather to Mrs. Crispe's newborn daughter.

Family Trade
The trade or business owned by the Narrator's father and now kept by Tom.

Court
The Court described as being in ill condition, with emulation, poverty, drinking, swearing, and loose amours.

Clergy
The clergy described as being so high that all people met by the Narrator protest against their practice; the clergy gave L33,743 to the Benevolence.

Benevolence
A voluntary contribution made by subjects to the sovereign; proved little, caused discontent, and the Narrator thinks to subscribe L20.

Exchange
Marketplace where the Office's bills were offered for sale at a 10 percent loss.

Office Bills
The bills held by the Office that were offered for sale on the Exchange at a ten percent loss.

Strange and Fatal Fevers
The fevers described in the passage as making the season very sickly everywhere.

Diary of Samuel Pepys, June/July/August 1661
Diary written by Samuel Pepys covering the months of June, July, and August 1661.

Project Gutenberg EBook
Electronic book that presents the diary text to readers.

John Pepys
Brother of Samuel Pepys; found in bed at eight o'clock, and his company wearies Samuel Pepys.

Pretty Dog
A dog that followed Samuel Pepys and that Samuel Pepys was tempted to steal.

Vow To Drink No Wine
A resolution made by Samuel Pepys to abstain from wine for the week.

Tom
Tom, also called Thomas and identified as Pepys’s brother, is the figure described throughout. He came to Pepys during the day, went with the narrator to the Bear Tavern and was given wine, and dined with the narrator while talking privately about the family trade and the London house. Tom was left in charge of maintaining his father’s trade, and the narrator feared that he would fail or “miscarry” for lack of brains and care. Tom also helped settle accounts.

In connection with marriage, Tom was the proposed husband for a broker’s daughter, described in other accounts as Mr. Evans’s daughter. The narrator and his father considered taking her as Tom’s wife, but the narrator feared the match would not take place. Overall, these descriptions present Tom as a brother engaged in the family business and as the subject of a doubtful marriage arrangement.

London
London is a central locale in the narrated account, serving as both a point of origin and a destination for travel. The narrator and his companions travel toward London by boat, and on one occasion the narrator rides on horseback to the city, where he finds his own household, his father's household, and My Lady all well. London is also the city from which the diarist set out on a journey to the house where he was staying, and from which Mr. Philips returns home toward the latter end of the week, after which the family seeks his counsel.

Within London, several notable events and associations occur. Mr. Moore is based in London when he sends advice to the narrator, and Father owns a house in the city. London is also the source of a hot venison pasty that was brought to Walthamstow. Additionally, the city is connected to religious observance: a form of prayer titled *A Form of Prayer* was to be used in London on the 12th of June, one of the special days appointed for the General Fast. The narrator traveled to London on the 22nd, reinforcing its role as a recurring destination in the diary narrative.

The Narrator
The Narrator is the unnamed first-person diarist and central figure of the diary account, and a member of the Pepys family. In addition to recording office business and daily life, he acts as deputy to My Lord and moves through London locations including the Wardrobe, Whitehall, Westminster Hall, the Privy Seal, Fleet Street, a tavern near the Savoy, Deptford, the theatre, Clerkenwell, and Bartholomew Fair. A specific diary entry for 11 and 12 June describes him going about business, writing to the Duke, meeting My Lord, and visiting several places.

The Narrator is also closely involved in family and estate matters. He is part of a family with his father, mother, uncle, and brother Tom, and he travels among Huntingdon, Brampton, Impington, Gravely, Graveley, Yelling, Offord, and Sturtlow. He reads over an uncle’s will, is engaged in a will dispute, negotiates with relatives and legal contacts, and arranges for the management of family lands. He treats friends at Magdalen, takes leave of cousin Angier, visits relatives, dines with Mr. Moore, and discusses public affairs. His left hand was recently stung and swollen, and he records personal concerns such as hoping for God’s forgiveness after breaking a vow to drink no wine.

The Narrator’s social and professional encounters include receiving a money offer from Mr. Shaw, going with My Lord from the Wardrobe and Whitehall to Deptford, and finally departing by wherry as the yacht salutes him. He records visits to his Lady, talks with his father and Mr. Evans, news of Lord Sandwich, meetings with departing travelers, a death, a marriage proposal, and outings to dinner and the theatre. Throughout, he remains an unnamed first-person observer who documents arguments, financial dealings, travel, family interactions, and public and private affairs.

Brampton
Brampton is a village closely associated with Samuel Pepys and his family, serving as a significant recurring location in his diary. The place is linked to the Pepys family through property and residence: Samuel Pepys’s father traveled there to settle and later lived in the village, and it was also the home of Robert Pepys, Samuel’s uncle, who lived and died in Brampton. The diarist himself repeatedly stayed, dined, and slept in the village with his father, and on at least one occasion rode there to find his father well, though he later returned home with a sad heart.

Brampton was a focus of family matters and business. Samuel’s father corresponded with him from Brampton, and a box containing Samuel’s uncle’s papers arrived from the village. The family spent several days there putting affairs in order and inspecting the fields, especially after Uncle Robert’s death, when the uncle’s corpse was at Brampton and his burial took place there. Property discussions also centered on Brampton: it was a place where the diarist intended to purchase property, and specifically where Mr. Norbury’s wife owned a house and land that were discussed with the narrator as a possible acquisition.

Additionally, Brampton served as a base for daily activities; the narrator and his father stayed there after walks and returned for supper and bed. The father was often alone in Brampton, prompting the diarist to write letters to him, and the father also planned or made trips there to settle matters before Samuel’s mother would come. The village thus functioned both as a family home and as a hub for estate and inheritance affairs during the period recorded in Pepys’s diary.

The King
The King, Charles II of England, is the monarch referenced throughout these diary entries. He was aboard his yacht at Greenwich when the narrator’s party arrived, and he was at Whitehall when My Lord took leave before beginning his journey; the Portuguese Ambassador also came to Whitehall to take leave of him. The King attended Sir William Davenant’s Opera, where the scene opened only after his arrival, and he was later present at the Theatre during the play “The Joviall Crew.” On another occasion, he attended the Opera with the Duke and Duchess of York, and the Duke planned to consult him about Navy money.

The King’s mistress at the time was Mrs. Palmer. Mr. Hill warned that the King would be forced to favour Presbytery, or the City would leave him. The King was expected to come and adjourn Parliament, and was later encountered on the water in his barge, on his way to adjourn the House. The previous day, he had participated in a stag hunt that tired out the horses of the other hunters. He also gave a billet to Clarendon and wrote a warrant naming Sir Stephen Fox. Finally, Mrs. Crispe intended to ask the King to be godfather to her daughter.

Pall
Pall, an individual associated with the household of the diarist (Samuel Pepys), appears in several accounts as a young woman and dependent relative. She attended the christening of Kate Joyce's child and stayed overnight at Pepys's father's house because she was feeling unwell. In another episode, she was taken by water with Lady Jem through the bridge to view ships and the diarist's house. She also joined the diarist, his wife, and Aunt Wight for supper at Aunt Wight's house.

Within the household, Pall was described as having grown proud and idle, leading the diarist to resolve not to keep her in his employment or care. He informed his own father that Pall should not remain with him any longer. At another point, he angrily declared he would keep her no more, while her father likewise refused to take responsibility for her. Because she was regarded as troublesome, she was eventually sent into the country with the diarist's mother and father. Prior to her departure, she was left to perform all the household work until another maid could be hired; thereafter, she was destined to go into the countryside with the diarist's mother. These various depictions together portray Pall as a source of tension within the household, leading to her removal from the diarist's immediate domestic sphere.

My Lady
“My Lady” is the woman referred to by that title in Samuel Pepys’s diary; she is a noblewoman associated with My Lord and was hostess at The Wardrobe. Pepys and his wife dined with My Lady and the children at the Wardrobe, where she showed them great hospitality and favour. The diarist visited her at her house on the 22nd, dined with her on several occasions—including at noon on April 28 and after meeting Uncle Wight—and accompanied Dean Fuller to a gathering at The Wardrobe where My Lady and the whole company were merry and well. In her husband’s absence, she returned to modest, poor housekeeping but continued to entertain.

Her close connections to the Pepys circle are reflected in the accounts. She was the mother of three sons who were sent to the narrator’s house. She mourned the death of her brother, Mr. Samuel Crew. Pepys supped with her while consulting about Lord Hinchingbroke’s illness, and he told her of My Lord’s sickness and recovery. He also informed her of Robert Pepys’s death. At another dinner at The Wardrobe, she called the diarist up to talk and innocently told him about Mrs. Crispe’s plan.

The Strand
The Bell at the Maypole, where Samuel Pepys met Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, Hartlibb, and Mr. Kipps, was located in the Strand.

Sir William Davenport
Sir William Davenport introduced the use of theatrical scenery.
